Verify Now Blog > Switching Power Supply PCB Design Guidelines and Best Practices Switching Power Supply PCB Design Guidelines and Best Practices by: Mila Nov 24,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout switching power supply switching power supply PCB design switching power supply design Switching power supplies are widely used in various electronic devices, ranging from industrial CNC equipment to compact consumer electronics. Compared with linear power supplies, switching power supplies offer higher conversion efficiency and flexible voltage regulation. However, their high-frequency switching operations also introduce design challenges related to noise, electromagnetic interference (EMI), and heat dissipation. Poor PCB layout can lead to excessive output ripple, electromagnetic interference, component overheating, or even circuit malfunctions, despite having a correct schematic. This article explores the main components of a switching power supply and explains key considerations for PCB component placement, current loops, grounding, EMI, and thermal management. 1. Four Main Components of a Switching Power Supply Before starting switching power supply PCB design, it is important to understand the main functional blocks of the circuit and their layout requirements. Different switching power supply topologies, such as Buck, Boost, and Flyback converters, have different circuit configurations. However, they can generally be analyzed in terms of the following four sections: 1. Input and output filter circuits 2. Switching control and driver circuits 3. Switching inductors or transformers 4. Output rectification and filter circuits Input and Output Filter Circuits The input filter circuit suppresses noise coming from the power input and reduces the impact of high-frequency currents generated by the switching circuit on the input power source. Input filter capacitors should generally be placed close to the input connector and power switching loop to shorten the current path. For high-frequency switching currents, the connection length and parasitic inductance between capacitors and power devices directly affect filtering performance. Therefore, related traces should be kept as short as possible, and input filter capacitors should not be placed far from the loops they need to supply with high-frequency current. (Compact Placement of Input Filter Capacitors) The image shows a compact input filter capacitor layout. Shortening the connections between the capacitors and the relevant circuit components helps reduce parasitic inductance and improve high-frequency filtering performance. Output filter capacitors should be placed close to the output of the rectifier or power inductor. This helps shorten the output current loop, reduce parasitic inductance, and minimize output ripple. Switching Control and Driver Circuits The switching control and driver circuits control the turn-on and turn-off of power MOSFETs and are essential to the proper operation of a switching power supply. The fast switching transitions of MOSFETs generate rapid changes in voltage and current, making the associated circuits potential sources of noise coupling and EMI. During PCB layout, particular attention should be paid to the routing of switching nodes. These nodes typically have a high rate of voltage change (dv/dt). Their copper area should be minimized, and they should be kept at an appropriate distance from feedback, sensing, and other sensitive signals. For example, in a flyback switching power supply (Flyback SMPS), the switching node connected to the MOSFET drain and the transformer primary winding typically experiences large voltage swings. In Buck and Boost converters, the SW node connecting the power switch and inductor also requires careful layout control. (Layout Separating High-Voltage Switching Nodes from Other Traces) The image shows a layout that separates switching nodes from other signal traces. High-voltage or high-frequency switching nodes should be kept away from optocouplers, feedback traces, and other sensitive circuits. Where necessary, PCB slots can be used in accordance with the circuit structure and insulation requirements. However, slots cannot replace proper electrical clearance, creepage distance, or insulation design. Feedback and voltage-sensing traces also require special attention. Switching power supply controllers rely on feedback signals to regulate the output voltage, making these traces susceptible to interference from switching noise. When routing these traces, consider the following: Keep feedback and sensing traces as short as possible to reduce noise coupling. Avoid routing feedback traces near noise sources such as MOSFETs, transformers, and inductors. Keep feedback traces away from high-frequency switching nodes and high-current traces. Select an appropriate reference ground based on the controller's feedback sensing method. Use Kelvin connections where necessary. · (Feedback Trace from the Optocoupler to the Driver) The image shows a dedicated feedback trace running from the optocoupler to the controller. Proper routing helps reduce interference from switching noise on the control circuit. In addition, peripheral components in the driver circuit, such as gate resistors, bypass capacitors, and RC filter networks, should be placed as close as possible to their corresponding driver pins. This shortens connection paths, reduces parasitic inductance, and improves switching control stability. Switching Inductors or Transformers Inductors and transformers are essential magnetic components in switching power supplies. Their placement affects power loop length, magnetic coupling, and the overall PCB layout. In Buck and Boost converters, the inductor is typically connected between the power switching stage and the output circuit. During PCB layout, high-current traces should be kept as short as possible. Sensitive signal traces should also be avoided between the inductor pads or directly beneath the inductor to reduce interference caused by magnetic coupling. (Switching Inductor) For isolated switching power supplies that use transformers, such as flyback converters, the transformer also provides electrical isolation between the input and output sides. Therefore, the primary and secondary windings must meet the clearance and creepage distance requirements specified by applicable safety standards. During PCB layout, avoid placing copper pours, traces, or unnecessary vias within the isolation barrier between the primary and secondary sides. For designs with limited space, PCB slots can be used to increase creepage distance when permitted by the insulation requirements. (PCB Slot Between Transformer Primary and Secondary Sides) The image shows a PCB slot used to increase the creepage distance between the transformer's primary and secondary sides. In an actual design, the required dimensions must also be determined according to the working voltage, overvoltage category, pollution degree, insulation class, and applicable safety standards. Output Rectification and Filter Circuits The output rectification circuit converts the pulsed voltage from the switching transformer or inductor into DC voltage. Depending on the power supply topology, the rectifier may use Schottky diodes, fast-recovery diodes, or synchronous rectification MOSFETs. When using Schottky diodes, their forward conduction losses and reverse-recovery characteristics should be considered. In high-current applications, the heat generated by the diodes can be significant. Therefore, the PCB copper area should be planned carefully to provide an effective heat dissipation path. Common PCB copper weights include 1 oz (approximately 35 μm) and 2 oz (approximately 70 μm). Increasing copper thickness generally helps reduce trace resistance and improve heat conduction. However, actual thermal performance also depends on copper area, board layer structure, the number of vias, and surrounding environmental conditions. For a two-layer PCB, copper areas can be extended around the component pads where appropriate. Multiple thermal vias can also be used to transfer heat to copper areas on the opposite layer, improving heat dissipation. (Schottky Diode Thermal Relief Area Using Bottom-Layer Copper) The image shows how bottom-layer copper can help dissipate heat from a Schottky diode. For higher-power components, thermal performance should also be evaluated through thermal simulation, actual temperature-rise testing, and additional external cooling structures where necessary. The filter capacitors after the output rectifier also require careful placement. Output capacitors should be positioned as close as possible to the relevant connection points of the rectifier and output inductor. This helps shorten the high-frequency current loop, reduce parasitic inductance, and minimize output ripple. (Short Current Loop Between Transformer Output, Rectifier Diode, and Filter Capacitor) The image shows a compact layout connecting the transformer output, rectifier diode, and filter capacitor. Shortening this loop helps reduce parasitic inductance and high-frequency voltage spikes, improving output power quality. 2. Key Layout Techniques for Switching Power Supply PCB Design Switching power supply PCB layout involves more than ensuring correct electrical connections between components. It also requires careful consideration of high-frequency current loops, signal integrity, grounding, and heat transfer. A well-planned layout can reduce noise coupling and EMI, minimize parasitic effects, and improve power supply stability. The following are some key aspects to consider. Output load ground: Provides the return path for load current. Control ground: Serves as the reference ground for the controller, feedback, and sensing circuits. Unless explicitly required by the circuit design, the two isolated sides must not be directly connected through ordinary copper pours or vias. If a high-frequency common-mode noise coupling path is required between the primary and secondary sides, a safety-compliant Y capacitor can be used as specified by the circuit design. A Y capacitor provides a controlled return path for high-frequency common-mode current, but it should not be used indiscriminately to eliminate DC potential differences between ground regions. For isolated power supplies that require a high-frequency coupling path between different ground regions, a Y capacitor can be used, provided that all applicable safety requirements are met. Avoid narrow return paths or unnecessary ground plane splits. Parasitic capacitance and noise coupling must still be controlled, especially around switching nodes. In switching power supplies, power switches and rectifiers generate large pulsed currents. If these currents share a high-impedance return path with the control circuit, additional voltage fluctuations may appear on the control ground, affecting feedback sensing and controller operation. It also requires careful consideration of component placement, high-frequency current loops, grounding, EMI, and thermal management. Output rectification and filter circuits Input and Output Filter Circuits The input filter circuit suppresses noise coming from the power input and reduces the impact of high-frequency currents generated by the switching circuit on the input power source. Input filter capacitors should generally be placed close to the input connector and power switching loop to shorten the current path. For high-frequency switching currents, the connection length and parasitic inductance between capacitors and power devices directly affect filtering performance. Therefore, related traces should be kept as short as possible, and input filter capacitors should not be placed far from the loops they need to supply with high-frequency current. (Compact Placement of Input Filter Capacitors) The image shows a compact input filter capacitor layout. Shortening the connections between the capacitors and the relevant circuit components helps reduce parasitic inductance and improve high-frequency filtering performance. Output filter capacitors should be placed close to the output of the rectifier or power inductor. This helps shorten the output current loop, reduce parasitic inductance, and minimize output ripple. The fast switching transitions of MOSFETs generate rapid changes in voltage and current, making the associated circuits potential sources of noise coupling and EMI. During PCB layout, particular attention should be paid to the routing of switching nodes. These nodes typically have a high rate of voltage change (dv/dt). Their copper area should be minimized, and they should be kept at an appropriate distance from feedback, sensing, and other sensitive signals. For example, in a flyback switching power supply (Flyback SMPS), the switching node connected to the MOSFET drain and the transformer primary winding typically experiences large voltage swings. In Buck and Boost converters, the SW node connecting the power switch and inductor also requires careful layout control. (Layout Separating High-Voltage Switching Nodes from Other Traces) The image shows a layout that separates switching nodes from other signal traces. High-voltage or high-frequency switching nodes should be kept away from optocouplers, feedback traces, and other sensitive circuits. Where necessary, PCB slots can be used in accordance with the circuit structure and insulation requirements. However, slots cannot replace proper electrical clearance, creepage distance, or insulation design. Feedback and voltage-sensing traces also require special attention. Switching power supply controllers rely on feedback signals to regulate the output voltage, making these traces susceptible to interference from switching noise. When routing these traces, consider the following: Keep feedback and sensing traces as short as possible to reduce noise coupling. Avoid routing feedback traces near noise sources such as MOSFETs, transformers, and inductors. Keep feedback traces away from high-frequency switching nodes and high-current traces. Select an appropriate reference ground based on the controller's feedback sensing method. Use Kelvin connections where necessary. · (Feedback Trace from the Optocoupler to the Driver) The image shows a dedicated feedback trace running from the optocoupler to the controller. Proper routing helps reduce interference from switching noise on the control circuit. In addition, peripheral components in the driver circuit, such as gate resistors, bypass capacitors, and RC filter networks, should be placed as close as possible to their corresponding driver pins. This shortens connection paths, reduces parasitic inductance, and improves switching control stability. Switching Inductors or Transformers Inductors and transformers are essential magnetic components in switching power supplies. Their placement affects power loop length, magnetic coupling, and the overall PCB layout. In Buck and Boost converters, the inductor is typically connected between the power switching stage and the output circuit. During PCB layout, high-current traces should be kept as short as possible. Sensitive signal traces should also be avoided between the inductor pads or directly beneath the inductor to reduce interference caused by magnetic coupling. Therefore, the primary and secondary windings must meet the clearance and creepage distance requirements specified by applicable safety standards. During PCB layout, avoid placing copper pours, traces, or unnecessary vias within the isolation barrier between the primary and secondary sides. For designs with limited space, PCB slots can be used to increase creepage distance when permitted by the insulation requirements. (PCB Slot Between Transformer Primary and Secondary Sides) The image shows a PCB slot used to increase the creepage distance between the transformer's primary and secondary sides. In an actual design, the required dimensions must also be determined according to the working voltage, overvoltage category, pollution degree, insulation class, and applicable safety standards. Depending on the power supply topology, the rectifier may use Schottky diodes, fast-recovery diodes, or synchronous rectification MOSFETs. In high-current applications, the heat generated by the diodes can be significant. Therefore, the PCB copper area should be planned carefully to provide an effective heat dissipation path. Common PCB copper weights include 1 oz (approximately 35 μm) and 2 oz (approximately 70 μm). Increasing copper thickness generally helps reduce trace resistance and improve heat conduction. However, actual thermal performance also depends on copper area, board layer structure, the number of vias, and surrounding environmental conditions. For a two-layer PCB, copper areas can be extended around the component pads where appropriate. Multiple thermal vias can also be used to transfer heat to copper areas on the opposite layer, improving heat dissipation. (Schottky Diode Thermal Relief Area Using Bottom-Layer Copper) The image shows how bottom-layer copper can help dissipate heat from a Schottky diode. For higher-power components, thermal performance should also be evaluated through thermal simulation, actual temperature-rise testing, and additional external cooling structures where necessary. The filter capacitors after the output rectifier also require careful placement. Output capacitors should be positioned as close as possible to the relevant connection points of the rectifier and output inductor. This helps shorten the high-frequency current loop, reduce parasitic inductance, and minimize output ripple. (Short Current Loop Between Transformer Output, Rectifier Diode, and Filter Capacitor) The image shows a compact layout connecting the transformer output, rectifier diode, and filter capacitor. PCB thermal management can be improved in several ways: Increase thermal copper area: Add copper around heat-generating components, such as power MOSFETs and rectifier diodes, according to their package and thermal requirements. Use thermal vias appropriately: Place thermal vias in suitable component pads or thermal copper areas to transfer heat to other copper layers. Optimize high-current traces: Increase trace width and copper thickness where necessary to reduce resistance and related power losses. Plan component spacing: Avoid placing multiple high-power components too close together, which can lead to localized heat buildup. Consider external cooling structures: For higher-power designs, add heatsinks or fans, or optimize the enclosure structure based on actual temperature-rise measurements. Note that a larger PCB copper area does not always result in better thermal performance. Electrical connections, parasitic capacitance, board layer structure, and actual cooling conditions must also be considered. For high-power switching power supplies, thermal simulation and prototype temperature-rise testing are recommended to verify the effectiveness of the thermal design. Conclusion Switching power supply PCB design involves more than ensuring correct electrical connections. It also requires careful consideration of component placement, high-frequency current loops, grounding, EMI, and thermal management. Controlling switching node areas, minimizing critical current loops, and providing appropriate heat dissipation paths for power components can help improve power supply efficiency, stability, and reliability. In practical designs, the layout should also be evaluated according to the specific topology, operating voltage, current, and applicable safety requirements to ensure that the PCB meets the product's performance and safety standards. USB Type-C Pinout: Why Are 5.1KΩ Pull-Down Resistors Needed? by: Mila Nov 09,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout USB Type-C pinout 5.1K pull-down resistor USB-C CC pin USB Type-C has become a common interface in modern electronic devices thanks to its reversible design, high-speed data transfer, and high-power delivery capabilities. However, in USB Type-C circuit design , a seemingly simple 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor plays an important role in device identification, connection detection, and power delivery. This article explains how the CC pins work, why two 5.1KΩ resistors are needed, and what to consider when designing a USB Type-C interface. Basic Functions of USB Type-C Pins: Understanding the CC Pins The CC (Configuration Channel) pins are among the most important pins in a USB Type-C connector. They are responsible for several key functions: Device Role Identification: Identify the power source (Source/DFP) and power sink (Sink/UFP). Plug Orientation Detection: Detect the orientation of the USB Type-C plug. Power Capability Identification: Determine the available default power level through the Rp resistor when USB PD is not used. USB PD Communication: Enable bidirectional communication through the CC pins for USB Power Delivery. VCONN Supply: Provide power to electronically marked cables equipped with E-Marker chips. （Type-C CC Pin） The Main Functions of the 5.1KΩ Pull-Down Resistor In a USB Type-C power sink (Sink/UFP), CC1 and CC2 typically each require a separate 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor (Rd) connected to ground. This is the standard resistor-based implementation of Rd and serves several important purposes. 1. Establishing a Defined CC Termination State The pull-down resistor provides a defined termination state for the CC pin. When a Source connects to a Sink, the Source-side pull-up resistor (Rp) and Sink-side pull-down resistor (Rd) form a detection circuit. By monitoring the voltage on the CC pin, the Source can determine whether a compatible Sink device has been connected. 2. Detecting Plug Orientation USB Type-C uses the CC1 and CC2 pins to detect plug orientation. Since the CC wire inside a standard Type-C cable connects to only one of the two CC pins, the Source can monitor their voltage states to identify which pin has an active connection. The interface controller then switches the corresponding data paths to ensure proper operation in either plug orientation. 3. Supporting Power Capability Identification The Source-side Rp and Sink-side Rd establish an electrical connection through the CC pin. By detecting the CC voltage, the Source can identify the connected Sink and determine the appropriate power delivery process. When USB PD is not used, the Source can also indicate its available default current capability through different Rp values. 4. Supporting USB PD Communication When both the Source and Sink support USB Power Delivery (USB PD), they can communicate bidirectionally through the CC pin to negotiate power voltage, current, and other supported functions. How Does the USB Type-C CC Pin Work? Voltage Divider Detection Mechanism The connection detection mechanism of a USB Type-C interface relies on the termination states of its CC pins. The Source-side CC pin is connected to a pull-up supply through Rp, while the Sink-side CC pin is connected to ground through a 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor (Rd). When the two devices are connected, these resistors form a voltage divider. For a resistor-based pull-up implementation, the CC voltage can be calculated using the following formula: Vcc = Vbus × (Rd / (Rp + Rd)) By monitoring the CC voltage, the Source can determine: Whether a compatible Sink device is connected. The type of connected termination. The orientation of the USB Type-C plug. The default power capability available to the Sink. Note that Rp can also be implemented using a current source instead of a resistor. Therefore, the formula above applies primarily to resistor-based pull-up implementations. USB Type-C Device Roles USB Type-C ports can operate in three main roles: Source (DFP): Supplies power and typically uses an Rp pull-up resistor or an equivalent current source for CC detection. Sink (UFP): Receives power and typically uses an Rd pull-down resistor (5.1KΩ) to establish the CC termination. Dual-Role Port (DRP): Can dynamically switch between Source and Sink roles depending on the connection. Plug Orientation Detection A USB Type-C connector has two CC pins, CC1 and CC2. However, in a standard cable connection, only one of them connects to the cable's CC wire. When the plug is inserted in one orientation, the cable's CC wire connects to CC1. When reversed, it connects to CC2. The Source monitors the voltage states of both pins to determine which one has an active connection and identify the plug orientation. The interface controller then switches the corresponding data paths based on the detected orientation, allowing the USB interface to work properly regardless of how the plug is inserted. Power Capability Identification (Without USB PD) Even without USB PD, a USB Type-C interface can indicate its available power capability through the Rp value on the CC pin. In addition to default USB current capabilities, a compliant Source can advertise 5V/1.5A or 5V/3A. These power levels are identified through different Rp resistance values or equivalent current-source implementations. Note: The voltage ranges above represent the corresponding detection ranges for the advertised current levels. Actual designs should follow the applicable USB Type-C specification and controller datasheets. Default USB current capability also depends on the USB connection type and its corresponding specification. Why Must the USB-C 5.1K Resistor Have This Specific Value? USB Type-C Standard Requirements For conventional USB Type-C Sink designs that implement Rd using resistors, 5.1KΩ is the standard pull-down resistance specified by the USB Type-C specification. It allows the Source to correctly identify the Sink connection and initiate the subsequent power delivery process according to the specification. It is important to note that the 5.1KΩ resistor alone does not mean the device supports USB PD communication. USB PD functionality also requires an appropriate protocol controller and physical-layer circuitry. Technical Reasons Specification Compliance: The 5.1KΩ value is the standard Rd resistance. It works with different Source-side Rp values to support the required connection detection mechanism. Reliable Detection: The appropriate pull-down resistance helps keep the CC voltage within the corresponding detection range, allowing the Source to correctly identify the Sink and its available power capability. Compatibility: Using non-standard values such as 10KΩ or 20KΩ may cause the CC voltage to fall outside the specified detection range, preventing some chargers or power sources from correctly identifying the Sink. Distinction from Ra: The USB Type-C specification also defines an Ra resistor, typically ranging from 800Ω to 1200Ω, which is used to identify cables requiring VCONN power. The clear difference between Rd and Ra helps the Source distinguish different connection states. Important Considerations in USB Type-C Circuit Design CC1 and CC2 Must Have Separate Resistors CC1 and CC2 must each have an independent 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor connected to GND. They should not share a single resistor. This is an easily overlooked detail in USB Type-C circuit design . If both CC pins share one pull-down resistor, neither pin can be guaranteed to have its own required Rd termination. When connecting a cable equipped with an E-Marker chip, the cable's Ra termination also participates in CC detection. Sharing one pull-down resistor may cause the Source to misinterpret the combination of Sink and Ra terminations, affecting device connection, cable identification, and VCONN supply. Resistor Tolerance and Package Selection For conventional resistor-based Rd implementations, a 5.1KΩ resistor with 1% tolerance is recommended to ensure stable resistance. Common package sizes include 0603 and 0805. The final selection depends on available PCB space, power dissipation, and assembly requirements. ﻿Common USB Type-C Design Mistakes 1. Missing Pull-Down Resistors: Without proper Rd termination, the Source may fail to detect the Sink device and initiate power delivery. 2. Sharing One Pull-Down Resistor: Connecting CC1 and CC2 to a single resistor may cause plug orientation detection problems and compatibility issues with some E-Marker cables. 3. Using the Wrong Resistance: Non-standard values such as 10KΩ or 20KΩ may cause the CC voltage to fall outside the specified detection range, affecting device identification and power delivery. A Classic Design Mistake: Raspberry Pi 4 （Raspberry Pi 4: Incorrect Type-C Output Pull-Down Resistor Design） The initial version of the Raspberry Pi 4 had a well-known USB Type-C design issue: CC1 and CC2 shared a single 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor instead of having separate pull-down resistors. This design did not comply with the USB Type-C specification. When connected to certain USB Type-C cables equipped with E-Marker chips, the Ra termination inside the cable could interact with the device's resistor network in an unexpected way. As a result, the power source could incorrectly identify the Raspberry Pi as an Audio Adapter Accessory and refuse to supply power. This case demonstrates how even a seemingly minor resistor connection error can affect the compatibility of an entire USB Type-C interface. Raspberry Pi addressed this issue in subsequent hardware revisions by separating the pull-down resistors for CC1 and CC2. （Type C sink; note that CC1 and CC2 are connected separately to 5.1k.） USB PD Communication Through the CC Pin Once the Source detects a valid connection through the 5.1KΩ Rd on the Sink side, it enables VBUS and provides the initial 5V supply. If both the Source and Sink support USB Power Delivery (USB PD), they can communicate bidirectionally through the CC pin to negotiate higher supply voltages (such as 9V, 15V, and 20V) and the corresponding current levels. USB PD uses BMC (Biphase Mark Coding) to transmit data through signal transitions on the CC pin. During this process, the 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor primarily establishes the Sink-side connection termination, while actual PD data communication is handled by the USB PD controller and its CC physical-layer circuitry. Therefore, the 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor is an important part of USB Type-C connection detection, but it is not the only requirement for USB PD communication. Conclusion Although the 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor is a simple passive component, it plays an important role in device identification, connection detection, and power compatibility in USB Type-C interfaces. Configuring separate Rd resistors for CC1 and CC2 allows Sink devices to establish connections according to the USB Type-C specification and communicate correctly with the Source. For PCB engineers, USB Type-C PCB design involves more than connecting data and power lines. Understanding how the CC pins work and properly configuring Rp and Rd resistors are equally important to avoiding device detection and power delivery issues. As USB Type-C and USB PD technologies continue to gain wider adoption, the CC pins remain essential for device connection, power negotiation, and cable identification. Getting these details right is fundamental to improving the reliability and compatibility of USB Type-C interfaces. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > What Is the Purpose of a 1MΩ Resistor in a Crystal Oscillator Circuit What Is the Purpose of a 1MΩ Resistor in a Crystal Oscillator Circuit by: Mila Nov 16,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB layout crystal oscillator circuit crystal oscillator circuit design crystal oscillator pcb layout crystal oscillator design In crystal oscillator circuit design , you may notice that some circuits include a 1MΩ resistor connected in parallel with the crystal, while others do not. Why is this resistor used, and what happens if it is omitted? Although both configurations can work normally, the feedback resistor can play an important role in establishing the proper operating conditions for reliable crystal startup. Two Common Crystal Oscillator Circuit Configurations In actual product development, you may encounter two different configurations when designing a crystal oscillator circuit. In Figure 1, there is no 1MΩ resistor connected in parallel with the crystal, while Figure 2 shows a 1MΩ resistor connected across the crystal. Figure 1: Crystal oscillator circuit with a parallel 1MΩ resistor Figure 2: Crystal oscillator circuit without a parallel 1MΩ resistor Problem Description In some circuit designs, the system operates normally when a 1MΩ resistor is connected in parallel with the crystal. However, without this resistor, the program may start slowly, run abnormally, or even fail to start. Why Is a 1MΩ Resistor Used in a Crystal Oscillator Circuit? 1. How Does the 1MΩ Feedback Resistor Work? In a typical Pierce crystal oscillator circuit, the MCU's internal inverter acts as an amplifier. For the circuit to oscillate reliably, the inverter must operate within its linear region, where it can provide sufficient gain. The 1MΩ resistor connected in parallel with the crystal serves as a feedback resistor. It provides a DC feedback path and helps establish a suitable bias point for the inverter without significantly loading the oscillation signal. 2. Why Can Some Crystal Oscillators Work Without a 1MΩ Resistor? Not every crystal oscillator circuit requires an external 1MΩ feedback resistor. Some MCUs already integrate the necessary feedback or bias circuitry. In these designs, the internal circuit can establish the appropriate operating point without an additional external resistor. However, if the feedback path is insufficient, the inverter may not operate at the intended bias point. This can result in: Slow crystal startup. Unstable oscillation. Failure to start. 3. How Does Temperature Affect Crystal Oscillator Startup? Temperature changes can affect both the crystal and the MCU's internal oscillator characteristics. For example, the crystal's equivalent series resistance (ESR) and the inverter's electrical characteristics may vary with temperature. These changes can reduce the oscillator's startup margin. If the oscillator loop cannot provide sufficient gain and negative resistance to overcome the crystal's ESR, startup may become slower or fail altogether. When troubleshooting such problems, check the MCU datasheet and reference circuit first. The crystal's ESR, load capacitance, and oscillator drive capability should also be evaluated. 4. Should a Series Resistor Be Added to the Crystal Circuit? Some crystal oscillator designs include a small series resistor, such as 100Ω, to limit the crystal's drive level or adjust the oscillator loop gain. However, this resistor is not required in every design. Its value depends on the crystal's drive-level specification, ESR, and the MCU's oscillator characteristics. An excessively large series resistance may reduce loop gain, making the crystal harder to start. Note: The feedback resistor and series resistor should not be selected arbitrarily. Always follow the MCU and crystal manufacturers' recommendations and verify startup reliability through testing under different operating temperature conditions. PCB Layout Considerations for Crystal Oscillator Circuits In addition to component selection, proper crystal oscillator PCB layout is essential for reliable operation. Consider the following points during crystal oscillator circuit design: Place the crystal as close as possible to the MCU's oscillator pins. Keep the traces between the crystal and load capacitors as short as possible. Minimize the loop area of the oscillator circuit. Keep high-speed signal traces, switching power supply nodes, and other potential noise sources away from the crystal circuit. Follow the chip manufacturer's reference layout when designing the ground plane beneath the crystal. Avoid applying a universal copper-pour rule without considering the specific oscillator design. Why Are Two MOSFETs Connected Back-to-Back in a MOSFET Circuit? by: Mila Nov 12,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout mosfet circuit MOSFET Body Diode Back-to-Back MOSFETs Bidirectional MOSFET Switch Reverse Current Blocking In PCB design , MOSFETs are widely used in power management circuits to control current flow, protect power sources, and manage power switching. However, when a circuit needs to support both charging and discharging while preventing unwanted reverse current, a single MOSFET may not be sufficient. This is where two back-to-back MOSFETs come into play. By connecting two MOSFETs in series with oppositely oriented body diodes, designers can create a bidirectional switch that allows current to flow in both directions when turned on and blocks current in either direction when turned off. This article explains how this configuration works and why it is useful in PCB power circuit design. 1. What Is a Bidirectional Switch? A bidirectional switch is a switching circuit built using MOSFETs, IGBTs, or other power semiconductor devices. It allows current to flow in either direction when turned on and blocks current in both directions when turned off. For example, when point A has a positive voltage and point B has a negative voltage, current can flow from A to B. When the voltage polarity reverses, with A becoming negative and B positive, the current direction also reverses, allowing current to flow from B to A. A bidirectional switch can be constructed by connecting two MOSFETs or IGBTs back-to-back. （Back-to-back MOSFET circuit） So, how does this configuration allow current to flow in both directions? 2. How Do Back-to-Back MOSFETs Enable Bidirectional Conduction? Let's use a circuit that supports both USB-to-battery charging and battery-to-USB power delivery as an example. Charging the Battery from USB When the USB power source charges the battery, the USB-side voltage is higher than the battery-side voltage. In this condition, Q3 turns on, and the USB power source establishes an initial current path through the body diode of Q1 and Q3. The control circuit then applies sufficient gate drive voltage to Q1 and Q2, turning both MOSFETs on. Once both MOSFETs are on, current flows through their conducting channels to the battery, allowing it to charge. Powering a USB Load from the Battery When the battery supplies power to an external USB load, the current flows in the opposite direction. Q3 turns on, allowing an initial current path to form through the body diode of Q2 and Q3. The control circuit then drives Q1 and Q2 on, allowing current to flow through both MOSFET channels toward the USB interface and power the external load. Blocking Reverse Current When Turned Off When Q3 is turned off, the charging and discharging paths are interrupted. The USB power source can no longer charge the battery, and the battery can no longer supply power to the external USB load. This provides reverse current blocking, also known as reverse current protection, preventing unwanted current from flowing back into the power source. It is important to note that the body diode does not automatically turn on the MOSFET channel. Actual MOSFET conduction depends on the gate-to-source voltage (VGS) and the control circuit's operating logic. （The Principle of Reverse Current Blocking） 3. Why Use Two Back-to-Back MOSFETs Instead of One? To understand this, we first need to look at an important MOSFET characteristic: the body diode. A MOSFET has an intrinsic body diode. In a typical N-channel enhancement-mode MOSFET, the body diode's anode is connected to the source (S), and its cathode is connected to the drain (D). This means that even when the MOSFET is turned off, its body diode can still conduct current under the right voltage conditions. Using a Single MOSFET When only one MOSFET is used, turning it off closes its conducting channel, but the body diode remains present. For example, suppose the battery is connected to the source side of the MOSFET and the external load is connected to the drain side. If the source voltage becomes higher than the drain voltage by enough to forward-bias the body diode, the diode conducts. Current can still flow from the battery to the external load through the body diode, so the MOSFET cannot fully block current in this direction. Therefore, a single MOSFET can conduct current in both directions when turned on, but it cannot block current in both directions when turned off. Using Two Back-to-Back MOSFETs When two MOSFETs are connected back-to-back, their body diodes face opposite directions. When both MOSFETs are turned on, their conducting channels are enabled, allowing current to flow from either side to the other. This provides bidirectional conduction. When both MOSFETs are turned off, the oppositely oriented body diodes provide bidirectional blocking. Regardless of which side has the higher voltage, one of the body diodes will be reverse-biased, preventing current from flowing through the series path. Therefore, two back-to-back MOSFETs can provide both bidirectional conduction and bidirectional blocking. Single MOSFET vs. Back-to-Back MOSFETs The main differences between these two configurations can be summarized as follows: （Single MOSFET vs. Back-to-Back MOSFETs） Conclusion Back-to-back MOSFETs provide an effective way to achieve bidirectional switching and reverse current blocking in power management circuits. Unlike a single MOSFET, this configuration can block current in either direction when turned off while allowing bidirectional conduction when both MOSFETs are on. For PCB design , understanding MOSFET body diode orientation and the operating states of each MOSFET is essential when designing battery charging and discharging circuits, power-path management systems, and other applications that require reliable current control. Proper component selection and gate-drive control are also important to ensure the circuit operates as intended. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Why Should a Decoupling Capacitor Be Placed Close to the IC Why Should a Decoupling Capacitor Be Placed Close to the IC by: Mila Nov 10,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout Decoupling Capacitor Decoupling Capacitor Placement Decoupling Capacitor Layout PCB Decoupling Capacitor “Decoupling capacitors should be placed as close to the IC as possible.” Almost every electronics design textbook emphasizes this rule. However, few explain exactly why the distance matters. If this is treated as a rule to memorize rather than a design principle to understand, it can be difficult to apply it effectively when layout problems arise. To understand why placement matters, we need to look at three key factors: parasitic inductance, capacitor equivalent series inductance (ESL), and current loop design. This article explores how decoupling capacitor placement affects circuit performance through simulation and practical PCB layout examples. 1. What Is a Decoupling Capacitor? The IC's Instantaneous Power Source Simply put, a decoupling capacitor (also known as a bypass capacitor) acts as a local energy storage unit. When an IC experiences a transient current demand, the capacitor can quickly supply the required current, helping maintain a stable supply voltage. When digital ICs switch logic states, their internal transistors switch rapidly and draw brief bursts of current from the power supply. If this current must be delivered entirely by a remote power source through long PCB traces, the parasitic inductance in the power and ground paths will oppose rapid changes in current. This can cause supply voltage drops, ground potential fluctuations, and other issues, including ground bounce. When a decoupling capacitor is placed close to the IC's power pin, the IC can draw charge from the nearby capacitor to meet transient current demands instead of relying entirely on the remote power supply. Because the current loop between the capacitor and the IC is shorter, its parasitic inductance is lower, helping reduce power supply voltage fluctuations. （A decoupling capacitor placed close to the IC supplies transient current during switching operations.） PCB traces between the capacitor and the IC inevitably introduce parasitic inductance. In general, the farther apart they are, the greater the parasitic inductance contributed by the traces. This trace-induced inductance is referred to as Lwire throughout this article. The trace inductance and the capacitor's own equivalent series inductance (ESL) jointly affect the entire decoupling loop. At high frequencies, inductive reactance increases with frequency, making it more difficult for the capacitor to deliver current quickly. In other words, the farther the capacitor is from the IC, the greater the parasitic inductance in the current loop is likely to be, and the less effective the capacitor becomes at high-frequency decoupling. 2. Capacitors Also Have Parasitic Inductance There is another important factor to consider: the capacitor itself has an equivalent series inductance (ESL), denoted as Lesl. A capacitor's ESL depends on its package size, internal construction, and mounting method. Generally, surface-mount ceramic capacitors have relatively low ESL because they do not have long leads. Through-hole capacitors, on the other hand, typically have higher ESL due to the additional inductance introduced by their leads and mounting paths. Because of ESL, every capacitor has an effective self-resonant frequency (SRF). The self-resonant frequency can be approximately calculated using the following formula: Where: L is the capacitor's equivalent series inductance (ESL). C is the capacitance. Below the self-resonant frequency, the capacitor behaves primarily as a capacitive element. At the self-resonant frequency, its impedance reaches a minimum. Above this frequency, the capacitor behaves primarily as an inductor. This is one reason why surface-mount ceramic capacitors are preferred for decoupling applications. Their relatively low ESL allows them to maintain capacitive behavior over a wider frequency range. The two parasitic inductances mentioned above—trace inductance Lwire and the capacitor's own ESL (Lesl)—can be modeled as series inductances in a simplified equivalent circuit. Together with the capacitance C, they form an LC network that affects the overall performance of the decoupling loop. In an actual PCB design, other parasitic elements introduced by the power and ground paths, pads, and vias must also be taken into account. (Equivalent circuit of a decoupling capacitor.) Trace parasitic inductance Lwire and the capacitor's equivalent series inductance Lesl jointly affect the high-frequency performance of the decoupling loop. 3. Simulation: How Does Placement Distance Affect Decoupling Performance? Varying the Distance Between the Decoupling Capacitor and the IC Simulation provides a straightforward way to observe how changes in capacitor placement distance affect power supply voltage fluctuations. The simulation parameters are as follows: Voltage source: Supply voltage VCC = 3.3 V. Current source: Simulates IC switching activity with a 1 ns rise time. Inductor: Represents the trace inductance Lwire between the IC and the capacitor. Decoupling capacitor: C = 0.1 μF, with an equivalent series inductance (ESL) of 1 nH. Measurement point: Voltage at the IC's power supply pin. (Simulation circuit schematic) Different placement distances between the IC and the capacitor are simulated by varying Lwire. （Simulation results with different trace inductance values） The simulation waveforms lead to the following conclusions: The closer the capacitor is to the IC, the smaller Lwire becomes. This generally reduces parasitic inductance in the current loop and improves power supply voltage stabilization. When the capacitor is placed too far away, additional trace inductance increases high-frequency impedance, reducing the capacitor's ability to respond to the IC's transient current demands. As trace inductance increases, the resonant frequency of the LC loop decreases, resulting in a longer ringing period. Varying the Capacitance Increasing capacitance helps suppress lower-frequency voltage fluctuations, but high-frequency performance does not necessarily improve due to ESL limitations. The simulation results show that increasing capacitance allows the capacitor to store more charge. Under otherwise identical conditions, this can help reduce voltage fluctuations at lower frequencies. However, this does not mean that a larger capacitor always provides better high-frequency decoupling. The capacitor's ESL limits its high-frequency performance. Once the operating frequency exceeds the self-resonant frequency, the capacitor behaves primarily as an inductor. Increasing capacitance alone may therefore not improve high-frequency decoupling. When selecting decoupling capacitors, capacitance should not be the only consideration. ESL and the target operating frequency must also be taken into account. 4. Multi-Level Decoupling for Better Power Integrity A single decoupling capacitor cannot effectively cover a wide frequency range. In practice, capacitors with different capacitance values are usually placed at different locations in the power distribution network to meet decoupling requirements across multiple frequency ranges. Level 1: At the PCB Power Input or Voltage Regulator Output (Energy Storage and Low-Frequency Support) These capacitors are typically placed near the power input or voltage regulator output. Their main functions include: Providing additional charge storage to support load variations. Reducing power supply voltage fluctuations at lower frequencies. Working with filtering circuits, when necessary, to suppress external power supply noise. Component selection: Aluminum electrolytic or tantalum capacitors with capacitance values in the tens of microfarads are commonly used. An LC filter can also be added when necessary. Level 2: Close to the IC Power Pins (High-Frequency Decoupling) These capacitors are placed close to the IC's power and ground pins. Their main functions include: Supplying local transient current during IC switching operations. Reducing the impedance of high-frequency current loops. Minimizing transient voltage fluctuations in the power and ground paths. Component selection: Surface-mount ceramic capacitors, typically ranging from 0.01 μF to 0.1 μF, are commonly used. Low-ESL models are preferred. The actual capacitance and number of capacitors should be determined based on the IC datasheet and power integrity requirements. As a general starting point, one decoupling capacitor per IC can be considered. For low-speed, low-current ICs, multiple devices may also share a single capacitor if the power distribution network and current loop are properly designed. The first level provides energy storage and low-frequency power support, while the second level suppresses high-frequency transient noise near the IC. 5. Practical PCB Decoupling Capacitor Layout Guidelines How Close Is Close Enough? As a general guideline, when space allows, the distance between a decoupling capacitor and the IC's power and ground pins should ideally be kept within 2–3 mm. However, this is only a practical reference for some conventional designs, not a universal design standard. For high-speed digital circuits, RF circuits, and other applications with demanding power integrity requirements, the layout recommendations provided by the IC manufacturer should take priority. It is also important to understand that physical proximity alone does not guarantee effective decoupling. What really matters is keeping the actual current path as short as possible. Even if a capacitor is physically placed right next to an IC, routing the power and ground traces along unnecessarily long paths can still create a large current loop. This increases parasitic inductance and reduces decoupling effectiveness. Conversely, even if there is a small physical gap between the components, a direct connection with a sufficiently short current loop can still provide good decoupling performance. When evaluating decoupling layouts, do not focus solely on the physical distance between components. Pay attention to the length of the complete current loop and its associated parasitic inductance. (Poor layout example) Although the components appear close together, winding traces unnecessarily extend the actual current path. The effectiveness of a decoupling capacitor should be evaluated based on the actual current loop. Pay Attention to the Ground Via In multilayer PCB designs, the via connecting the capacitor's ground terminal to the ground plane should be placed as close as possible to the capacitor's ground pad. When the design allows, the via can be placed directly next to the pad or implemented using an appropriate via-in-pad design. If the via is too far from the pad, the connecting trace also introduces parasitic inductance, increasing the impedance of the current loop. When space permits, one or more ground vias can be placed near the capacitor's ground pad to shorten the connection to the ground plane. At the same time, avoid unnecessary vias or routing between the IC's power pin and the decoupling capacitor to keep the entire current loop as short as possible. Conclusion Effective decoupling requires more than simply placing a capacitor near an IC. Capacitance, ESL, placement, and current loop design all affect power supply stability. By understanding how these factors interact and applying proper PCB layout techniques, you can reduce power supply noise and improve overall circuit performance. AI Pyramid Computing Box Pro 8GB Version PCB Ground Plane Design: Routing Across Plane Splits and Signal Return Paths Talking about the Composition of PCB Price Over the years, PCB price changes have been familiar with people inside and outside the industry, even though some people with years of experience in the PCB industry may not fully understand the ins and outs of this, so to analyze the main factors affecting pcb price: The diversity of prices caused by the different materials used in PCBs is based on common double-sided boards. Sheets generally include fr-4, cem-3, etc., and board thickness varies from 0.2mm to 5.0mm, and copper thickness varies from 0.5oz to 3oz. All of these have resulted in huge price differences on the sheet material; in solder mask inks, there are also certain price differences between ordinary thermoset oils and photosensitive green oils, and thus the diversity of materials has caused price diversity. The different production processes used by PCBs result in different production processes with different prices that will result in different costs. Such as gold-plated plates and sprayed tin plates, the production of the shape of the milling (milling) plate and beer (red) plate, the use of silk screen lines and dry film lines will have different costs, resulting in a variety of prices. The diversity of prices caused by the difficulty of the PCB itself Even if the material is the same, the process is the same, but the difficulty of the PCB itself will result in different costs. For example, if there are 1000 holes on both boards, the hole diameter of one board is more than 0.6mm and the hole diameter of the other board is less than 0.6mm, different drilling costs will be formed; if the two boards are the same, the linewidth is different. Differently, one type is larger than 0.2mm and one type is smaller than 0.2mm, which also causes different production costs, because the scrap rate of difficult plates is high, the inevitable cost is increased, and the price diversity is thus caused. Different customer requirements will also cause different prices The level of customer demand will directly affect the plate production rate, such as a board by ipc-a-600e, class1 requirements have a 98% pass rate, but according to class3 requirements may be only 90% The passing rate, resulting in different costs for the mill, eventually led to a change in the price of the product. The diversity of prices caused by different PCB manufacturers even if the same product, but because of different manufacturers of technology and equipment, different levels of technology, will also form a different cost, nowadays many manufacturers like to produce tin spray plate, because the process is simple, low cost, but Some manufacturers also produce gold-plated plates, resulting in higher scrap rates and higher costs. Therefore, they prefer to produce tin-spray plates, so their prices for tin-spray plates are lower than those for gold-plated plates. The price difference caused by different payment methods At present, PCB manufacturers generally adjust PCB prices according to different payment methods, ranging from 5% to 10%, which also results in price differences. Diversification of prices caused by regional differences At present, from the geographical point of view, prices have been increasing from south to north. There are certain differences in prices in different regions, and thus different regions have also caused price diversity.
