events.after: Resources / Machining Design / Dry Etching vs. Wet Etching - Differences and Applications Dry Etching vs. Wet Etching - Differences and Applications Written by Catalin-Daniel Neagu Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 10 min read Published March 1, 2022 Updated November 20, 2026 Explore the differences and applications of dry etching and wet etching The choice between dry and wet etching is an early decision in semiconductor and microfabrication processes when defining patterning and material-removal steps. Many considerations must be taken into account to decide which etching method to use on a wafer when creating electronic components, whether it employs liquid etchants (wet etching) or gaseous species in plasma form (dry etching). This article explains the dry and wet etching processes, their methods, and key applications. We will also clarify the differences between them and the main factors to consider when choosing between the two. If you'd like to learn more about other types of part markings, you can also visit our guide on direct part marking. Etching Definition Etching is a manufacturing technique used to remove layers or slices of a workpiece, including semiconductors, dielectrics, polymers, and metals. It can employ chemical corrosion, electrochemical reactions, or physical processes such as ion bombardment. Different etching processes are used depending on the desired manufacturing outcome. The procedure for different applications can vary greatly in terms of etching chemicals, the temperature used in the process, and exposure time. Safety is also a concern because fumes and vapors from wet etching chemicals can cause corrosion and health hazards if not properly contained or ventilated. It’s also important to take proper precautions when handling cleaning solvents used after liquid immersion or vapor-phase processing. Etching Considerations and Performance Parameters Before comparing wet and dry etching, it helps to understand how etching performance is evaluated. Applying a liquid or vapor etchant causes complex molecular interactions that significantly affect the material’s surface. Regardless of the type of etching we are talking about, an etching treatment can cause one of three outcomes: Isotropic etching: The material is removed uniformly in all directions, creating a rounded profile or undercut beneath the mask. Since it’s a less precise form of etching, isotropic processes are used mainly for material removal and surface smoothing, not for cleaning, which is typically done using chemical cleans rather than etching. Completely anisotropic etching: The material is removed primarily in the vertical direction, producing sidewalls that are nearly vertical when viewed in cross-section. Anisotropic etching: The created shape has a form between the two mentioned above. Anisotropic etching is commonly used to create circuit patterns. Manufacturers evaluate several key performance parameters to determine the best etching method, whether wet or dry: Etching rate: the speed at which etching occurs, or the thickness being etched per unit of time. It is usually measured in μm/min or nm/min (micrometers or nanometers per minute). Selectivity: the ratio of the etch rate of the target material to that of the mask or another material (R_target / R_mask). It is crucial for determining how well the mask can withstand the process when defining or choosing the mask. Etch uniformity: the etch rate variation throughout one part, multiple parts, or multiple batches of parts. It is commonly expressed as (R_max − R_min) / (R_max + R_min), describing how uniformly the material is removed across a wafer or batch. Anisotropy: defined as the etching directionality, meaning that when A=0, the etching is considered isotropic, and when A=1, the process is completely anisotropic. The Wet Etching Process Wet etching is a technique that uses a liquid solution (usually called an etchant in the liquid phase) to remove layers or portions of a workpiece, such as a silicon wafer. This process is widely used in semiconductor fabrication for wafer manufacturing and treatment. The main advantage of using it is the ability to conduct surface removal on a part-wide scale. Wet etching is often used to remove specific layers or defects on the wafer surface, rather than intrinsic impurities, which are typically controlled through doping or material growth processes. Etchants corrode the material, and this corrosion is controlled by masks. Masks are materials that resist the etchant, protecting specific regions of the wafer to define the pattern or feature geometry. However, the etch depth is controlled by the etch duration and rate, while the channel width can be roughly estimated as the mask opening plus twice the etch depth. Common mask materials include photoresist, silicon dioxide (SiO₂), silicon nitride (Si₃N₄), and occasionally metals such as chromium or gold, depending on the substrate and etchant used. In wet etching, engineers typically use acids such as hydrofluoric, nitric, phosphoric, and hydrochloric. The advantages of these etchants lie in their chemical selectivity and ability to achieve uniform removal rates for specific materials. Types of Wet Etching Wet etching can be performed using several configurations, most commonly immersion (dip), spray, or spin etching: In the dip or immersion method, wafers are submerged in a tank containing the etchant solution. This traditional approach is widely used for batch processing and allows multiple wafers to be etched simultaneously. In spray or spin etching, the wafer is rotated while the etchant is sprayed onto its surface to enhance uniformity and reduce chemical usage. The setup typically includes a collection system for spent chemicals, not an absorption mechanism. The rotation primarily improves uniformity and distribution of the etchant, while the etch rate itself depends on the crystal orientation of the substrate, particularly in anisotropic etchants like KOH or TMAH. Immersion etching remains the most common method for silicon wafers, while spray or spin systems are preferred when improved chemical control or reduced consumption is needed. The choice depends on material and safety considerations, not simply on acidity. Silicon wet etching in semiconductor fabrication can use either immersion or spray methods, though immersion in aqueous alkaline solutions such as KOH or TMAH is most common. It’s a misconception that wet etching always relies on immersion baths; spray and single-wafer systems are also used, particularly for modern cleanroom tools where chemical consumption and uniformity are tightly controlled. The Dry Etching Process Dry etching encompasses several techniques, many of which use plasma. While the term ‘plasma etching’ is sometimes used broadly, it refers more specifically to processes where chemical reactions dominate rather than purely physical sputtering. Dry etching removes material from the surface using energetic ions or reactive species generated in plasma or ion beams. Those beams contain high-energy particles (in the form of ionized gases in the plasma phase) that dislodge surface atoms, which are then removed as volatile reaction products or by physical sputtering. The etched area is then controlled via masked patterns. The process allows for high aspect ratio geometry creation. This technique is also widely used in semiconductor fabrication. Dry etching is preferred for its reduced undercutting and its ability to produce anisotropic, high-aspect-ratio features. Etch uniformity depends on process parameters such as gas composition, pressure, plasma density, and electrode geometry. The etched profile is strongly influenced by the specific technique used. Typical gases used in this process include oxygen, fluorocarbons, and chlorine and bromine species (in the plasma phase). Hydrogen plasmas have been investigated for surface cleaning, damage removal, and certain compound semiconductor etches, but their use remains specialized. Oxygen plasma is primarily used to etch or clean organic materials and polymers. It is generally ineffective on metals unless combined with other chemistries or used for oxide formation rather than etching. Types of Dry Etching Different plasma manipulation techniques and equipment give rise to several types of dry etching: Ion beam etching (IBE): the most straightforward of the dry etching processes. It directs argon ions onto the surface as an ion beam at energies of 1-3 keV (kiloelectronvolts). These energies are sufficient to sputter material from the surface, hence the use of ion sources to generate the beam. Reactive ion etching (RIE): a type of dry etching that makes use of chemically reactive species (reactive ions) that are accelerated toward a substrate (in most cases a silicon wafer). Inside the etching chamber, the wafer is placed on an RF-powered electrode that biases the ions and controls their directionality toward the surface. This allows highly anisotropic channels to form. By increasing pressure in the etching chamber, the mean free path of particles can be reduced, which translates into a less directional etching, resulting in a more isotropic channel. ICP-RIE etching (or simply ICP etching): uses an inductively coupled plasma source. The plasma is generated with an RF-powered electromagnetic field and added to a conventional RIE system, allowing greater control over plasma density and ion energy. Plasma etching: a subclass of dry etching capable of creating isotropic etch profiles. It is often used to remove whole film layers. In plasma etching, the substrate is exposed mainly to neutral radicals and low-energy ions that chemically react with the surface, so the process is generally more isotropic than RIE. Many dry etching processes are plasma-based, so the terms are sometimes used interchangeably, although not all dry etching relies on plasma chemistry. Considering the techniques described above, dry etching methods can be further categorized as follows: Chemical reaction processes: those that use plasma or reactive gases (plasma etching). Physical removal processes: that make use of momentum transfer to knock off material (IBE). A combination of the two above (RIE and ICP etching). Reactive gases used in dry etching, such as fluorocarbons and chlorine compounds, pose chemical and toxicity hazards. However, these processes are conducted in sealed vacuum systems with exhaust scrubbing, which minimizes operator exposure. While more complex than wet etching, dry etching allows precise patterning and surface modification of wafers through controlled chemical and physical reactions. Dry Etching vs. Wet Etching After understanding both processes, the key differences and applications between dry and wet etching can be compared. Generally speaking, wet etching uses simpler equipment, is less complex, and typically achieves higher etch rates than dry etching. It's also more highly selective. However, wet etching also requires larger chemical volumes and poses greater handling and contamination risks compared to dry etching, and it offers less control over feature geometry. Dry etching, on the other hand, offers strong anisotropic control, higher precision, and generally safer operation within sealed vacuum systems. Depending on the process, dry etching can achieve moderate to high etch rates while consuming less reagent volume than wet processes. However, it is a more complex process, requiring more sophisticated equipment, and it offers lower selectivity. Both techniques are widely used in: Semiconductor fabrication Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems (MEMS) production PCB fabrication (primarily wet etching) Thin-film and metal micro-etching Transistor gate patterning (primarily dry etching) Both techniques use etchants, either in gas or liquid form, to remove material from part surfaces. Silicon processing is the most common use case. With anisotropy being critical in micro- and nano-scale semiconductor structures, dry etching offers many advantages over wet etching for precision pattern transfer. "The choice between dry and wet etching often comes down to control versus simplicity. Wet etching remains unmatched for throughput and ease, but when geometry precision or feature definition really matters, dry etching is the engineer’s most reliable tool." Audrius Zidonis PhD Principal Engineer at Zidonis Engineering Etching with Xometry Both dry and wet etching play crucial roles in modern manufacturing, especially in microelectronics and semiconductor fabrication. Dry and wet etching are essential in electronics manufacturing, each suited to different project requirements. The main difference between them lies in the state and mechanism of the etchant: liquid-phase chemistry for wet etching versus plasma or ion-based reactions for dry etching. events.before: Resources / Machining Design / How Does a Hydraulic System Work How Does a Hydraulic System Work Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 19 min read Published November 24, 2026 Updated November 25, 2026 A hydraulic system works by using pressurized fluid to transmit force from one point to another, enabling machines to perform heavy mechanical tasks with precision and control. The hydraulic system operates on Pascal's Law, which states that pressure applied to a confined fluid transmits equally in all directions, allowing a small input force to generate a significantly larger output force at the actuator. Hydraulic systems appear in excavators, aircraft landing gear, industrial presses, and injection molding machines because the fluid medium delivers a consistent, controllable force regardless of load orientation. Hydraulic systems are used in machines because they produce far greater force-to-size ratios than purely mechanical or pneumatic alternatives, with operating pressures commonly ranging from 1,000 psi to 5,000 psi in industrial equipment. The system type determines the application, with open-center, closed-center, and hydrostatic configurations each serving distinct operational requirements. A pump, reservoir, control valves, actuator, and hydraulic fluid form the core methodology through which energy converts into mechanical motion. The primary benefits include high power density, smooth speed control, overload protection through pressure relief valves, and the ability to transmit force over long distances without mechanical linkages. 1. Pump Pushes Fluid From Reservoir A hydraulic pump draws fluid from the reservoir and forces it into the system, converting mechanical energy into hydraulic flow. Gear, vane, and piston pumps generate flow rates from 1 GPM to over 100 GPM, depending on system size. Without continuous fluid displacement from the pump, no pressure builds, and no actuator movement occurs. 2. Input Force Creates Pressure Resistance encountered by the flowing fluid creates pressure within the system, measured in psi or bar. Pressure originates from the load or restriction opposing fluid flow at the actuator or control valve, not from the pump directly. A pump rated at 3,000 psi reaches that pressure only when the system load demands it. 3. Pressure Travels Through Fluid Pressurized fluid transmits force through hoses, tubes, and fittings with negligible energy loss over distance. Pascal's Law confirms that pressure applied at one point in a sealed fluid system transmits equally to every connected surface. Steel tubing rated to 6,000 psi and hydraulic hoses rated from 1,500 psi to 10,000 psi carry the pressurized fluid safely. 4. Fluid Reaches Actuator Directional control valves route pressurized fluid to the correct actuator port, determining whether the cylinder extends, retracts, or holds position. Fluid volume delivered to the actuator determines travel speed, while pressure determines the applied force. A closed-center valve locks the actuator in position when no command signal is present. 5. Actuator Produces Movement The actuator converts hydraulic pressure into mechanical force or motion through a cylinder or hydraulic motor. A double-acting cylinder with a 4-inch bore at 2,500 psi generates approximately 31,416 pounds of push force. Return fluid travels back to the reservoir after the stroke completes, finishing the closed-loop cycle. What Is a Hydraulic System? A hydraulic system is a power transmission technology that uses pressurized incompressible fluid to generate, control, and deliver mechanical force to actuators performing physical work. The system operates on Pascal's Law, established in 1647, confirming that pressure on a confined fluid transmits equally in all directions. Standard industrial hydraulic systems operate at 1,000 psi to 5,000 psi, with specialized systems reaching 10,000 psi to 15,000 psi in aerospace applications. The fluid serves simultaneously as the power carrier, lubricant, and heat transfer agent, distinguishing hydraulic systems from mechanical or pneumatic alternatives. Petroleum-based hydraulic oil with viscosity grades from ISO VG 32 to ISO VG 68 fills the reservoir, pump, valve block, and actuator circuit continuously during operation. Force multiplication through piston area ratios makes it possible to lift loads exceeding 50 tons using a compact pump driven by a 50-horsepower motor. Hydraulic systems serve aerospace, construction, manufacturing, agriculture, and marine industries because no equivalent technology delivers the same combination of force density, controllability, and design flexibility. What Are the Main Components of a Hydraulic System? The main components of a hydraulic system are listed below. Hydraulic Reservoir : The reservoir stores hydraulic fluid from 5 gallons to over 500 gallons, dissipates heat from returning fluid, and provides a steady supply to the pump inlet without cavitation. Hydraulic Pump : The pump converts mechanical energy into hydraulic flow, with gear, vane, and piston pumps covering flow ranges from 1 GPM to 150 GPM at pressures from 1,500 psi to 6,000 psi. Control Valves : Directional, pressure relief, and flow control valves manage fluid routing, maximum operating pressure, and actuator speed. Pressure relief valves are set from 500 psi to 5,000 psi to prevent system overpressure. Actuators : Hydraulic cylinders and motors convert fluid pressure into mechanical force or torque. A cylinder with a 3-inch bore at 2,000 psi generates approximately 14,137 pounds of linear force. Hydraulic Fluid : Petroleum-based or synthetic fluid transmits pressure while lubricating internal surfaces. ISO VG 46 is the most commonly specified viscosity grade for industrial systems operating at 40°C to 80°C. Filters and Seals : Filters rated at 3 to 25 microns remove particulate contamination, while seals prevent leakage at pressures up to 6,000 psi. Is the Pump Responsible for Creating Flow in the System? Yes, the pump creates flow in a hydraulic system, but it does not directly create pressure. The pump displaces a fixed or variable volume of fluid per revolution, establishing a flow rate in GPM. Pressure develops only in response to the resistance the flowing fluid encounters at the load, actuator, or closed valve. A gear pump at 1,800 RPM with 0.5 cubic inches per revolution displacement delivers approximately 3.9 GPM regardless of system pressure. Increasing pump speed raises flow and actuator speed, while increasing system load raises pressure without changing pump flow rate. Variable displacement piston pumps adjust output volume automatically in response to system demand, reducing flow to near zero when the actuator reaches full extension and maintaining standby pressure from 200 psi to 500 psi without energy waste. The pump originates all fluid movement in the circuit, and load resistance downstream transforms that movement into working pressure that performs mechanical work. Why Are Hydraulic Systems Used in Machines? Hydraulic systems are used in machines because they deliver exceptionally high force output relative to component size, a characteristic no purely mechanical or electromechanical system matches at equivalent scale. A hydraulic cylinder with a 6-inch bore at 3,000 psi produces over 84,823 pounds of force from a unit weighing under 50 pounds. Machines rely on hydraulic systems for precise, stepless speed and force control across variable output ranges. A proportional flow control valve adjusts actuator speed continuously from 0 to maximum, giving operators exact positioning authority over loads exceeding several tons without discrete steps or complex mechanical transmissions. Hydraulic systems also provide inherent overload protection through pressure relief valves preset from 1,500 psi to 5,000 psi, redirecting excess fluid to the reservoir automatically when an overload occurs. No operator intervention is required to protect downstream components. The combination of high force density, smooth controllability, and overload protection explains why construction excavators, aircraft control surfaces, industrial presses, and agricultural equipment all depend on hydraulic power as a core engineering solution. How Do Hydraulic Machines Multiply Force? Hydraulic machines multiply force by applying pressure across different piston surface areas within the same sealed circuit, following Pascal's Law, where Force equals Pressure multiplied by Area (F = P × A). A small pump piston generating 2,000 psi transmits that exact pressure to a large actuator cylinder, where the greater surface area produces a proportionally larger output force. A pump piston with a 1-square-inch area receiving 100 pounds of input generates 100 psi system pressure. Acting on a cylinder bore with a 20-square-inch area, the same 100 psi produces 2,000 pounds of output force, a 20-to-1 multiplication ratio. The trade-off is travel distance: the large cylinder moves a shorter distance than the input piston for the same fluid volume displaced. Hydraulic press systems in metal stamping exploit the multiplication principle at an industrial scale, with cylinder bore diameters reaching 24 inches at 3,000 psi to generate forces exceeding 1,000 tons. The force multiplication ratio scales directly with the actuator-to-pump piston area ratio across every application size. Are Hydraulic Systems More Powerful Than Mechanical Systems of the Same Size? Yes, hydraulic systems are more powerful than mechanical systems of the same physical size. A hydraulic motor delivering 50 horsepower occupies approximately one-third the volume and one-fourth the weight of a mechanical gearbox transmitting equivalent power at the same output torque. Hydraulic actuators achieve force levels of tens of thousands of pounds from cylinders compact enough to fit inside a vehicle chassis or aircraft wing, where no mechanical alternative packages equally. Energy travels at pressures from 1,000 psi to 5,000 psi through hoses and compact valves, eliminating the rigid shafts, gears, and bearings that add mass to mechanical power trains. Mechanical systems maintain efficiency advantages in steady-state transmission, with spur gear drives reaching 95% to 99% efficiency compared to 70% to 85% for hydraulic systems due to fluid friction and internal leakage losses. The efficiency gap narrows in variable-speed applications where hydraulic systems avoid throttling losses of fixed-ratio mechanical drives, confirming that power density and application context together determine which technology performs better at a given size. Why Are Hydraulic Fluids Important in Hydraulic Systems? Hydraulic fluids are important because the fluid simultaneously serves as the energy transmission medium, internal lubricant, heat transfer agent, and sealant across the entire operating cycle. No other single element performs as many simultaneous functions, making fluid selection and condition directly responsible for system performance and component service life. The fluid transmits pressure with minimal compressibility, quantified by a bulk modulus ranging from 200,000 psi to 300,000 psi for petroleum-based hydraulic oils. The high bulk modulus ensures pressure changes at the pump translate immediately into actuator force without energy absorption lag. The fluid also lubricates pump gears, valve spools, and cylinder surfaces, with viscosity maintained from ISO VG 32 to ISO VG 68 at operating temperatures from 40°C to 80°C. Heat generated by pressure drops across valves and pump friction accumulates in the fluid, which carries thermal energy to the reservoir and heat exchanger for dissipation. Contaminated or degraded Hydraulic Fluids account for 70% to 80% of all hydraulic system failures, confirming that fluid condition governs overall system reliability more than any other maintenance variable. How Do Hydraulic Fluids Transfer Power in Industrial Machines? Hydraulic fluids transfer power in industrial machines by acting as an incompressible medium that carries pressure energy from the pump through the valve circuit to the actuator with minimal energy loss. The fluid fills the entire enclosed circuit continuously, meaning pressure generated at the pump reaches the cylinder or motor in milliseconds, regardless of circuit distance. Power transfer efficiency depends on fluid viscosity at operating temperature. Viscosity too low allows internal leakage across pump and valve clearances of 0.001 inch to 0.003 inch, dropping volumetric efficiency below 90% and wasting output as heat. Viscosity too high increases flow resistance and pressure drop across valve passages. ISO VG 46 at 50°C maintains approximately 46 centistokes, balancing leakage control with acceptable flow resistance in most industrial applications. Additive packages in industrial fluids improve transfer reliability by preventing oxidation, foam, and surface wear. Anti-wear additives containing zinc dialkyldithiophosphate (ZDDP) protect pump pistons and valve lands operating under contact pressures from 50,000 psi to 200,000 psi, maintaining the dimensional precision that volumetric efficiency requires throughout the service interval. Are Hydraulic Fluids Essential for Pressure and Lubrication Control? Yes, hydraulic fluids are essential for pressure control and lubrication, and neither function operates independently. The same fluid transmitting working pressure from 1,000 psi to 5,000 psi simultaneously lubricates every internal moving surface it contacts within the pump, valves, and actuator. Pressure control depends on fluid incompressibility. Petroleum-based hydraulic oil compresses less than 0.5% per 1,000 psi of applied pressure, making it an effective transmission medium that responds to load changes without absorbing significant energy. Degraded fluid with a reduced bulk modulus slows pressure response and decreases actuator positioning accuracy measurably. Lubrication control depends on maintaining adequate viscosity at operating temperature. Pump pistons, shoes, and swash plates rely on a hydrodynamic fluid film of 1 to 10 micrometers to prevent metal-to-metal contact at relative surface velocities from 1 to 10 meters per second. Allowing fluid viscosity to drop below 10 centistokes at maximum operating temperature collapses the film and reduces pump service life from 10,000 hours to below 2,000 hours. How Do Plastic Injection Molding Machines Use Hydraulic Systems? Plastic injection molding machines use hydraulic systems to generate and control the forces required for mold clamping, plastic injection, pack hold, and part ejection, with each phase demanding precise force and speed control at production cycle times of seconds per shot. The clamping unit uses large-bore hydraulic cylinders with bore diameters from 8 inches to 24 inches to hold mold halves closed against injection pressure. A mold with a 100-square-inch projected area at 15,000 psi injection pressure requires at least 750 tons of clamping force to prevent flash formation at the parting line. The hydraulic clamp cylinder generates equivalent force at system pressures from 2,000 psi to 3,500 psi through piston area advantage. The injection unit drives the screw forward at velocities from 50 mm per second to 500 mm per second, forcing molten polymer through runners and gates at fill pressures from 10,000 psi to 30,000 psi. Proportional hydraulic valves control injection speed and holding pressure independently during each phase, giving process engineers the precision needed to maintain dimensional tolerances in Plastic Injection Molding Machines producing parts to ±0.001-inch specifications. Why Is Hydraulic Pressure Critical in Plastic Injection Molding Machines? Hydraulic pressure is critical in plastic injection molding machines because every phase of the cycle requires a distinct pressure level, and the hydraulic system must switch from one to another within milliseconds to maintain part quality and dimensional consistency. Hydraulic pressure from 2,000 psi to 3,500 psi must exceed the separating force generated by melt pressure inside the cavity during clamping. Insufficient clamp pressure causes flash defects at the parting line, while excess pressure accelerates mold wear. During injection, hydraulic pressure drives fill at 10,000 psi to 30,000 psi and then maintains pack pressure from 5,000 psi to 15,000 psi to compensate for polymer shrinkage during cooling. Pack pressure directly controls part weight, sink mark depth, and dimensional stability. A 5% variation in pack pressure produces measurable changes in part mass and feature dimensions for precision components (medical device housings and optical lenses). Pressure consistency across thousands of cycles, maintained by closed-loop hydraulic control, determines whether the machine produces parts within specification across high-volume production runs. Do Plastic Injection Molding Machines Rely on Hydraulic Force for Clamping? Yes, plastic injection hydraulic molding machines rely on hydraulic force for clamping, with clamp cylinders generating forces from 5 tons to over 4,000 tons through direct-acting or toggle-assisted hydraulic arrangements. A direct hydraulic clamp uses a single large-bore cylinder behind the moving platen to generate clamping force directly from hydraulic pressure. A toggle clamp uses a hydraulic cylinder to actuate a mechanical linkage that multiplies cylinder force by a ratio of 20:1 to 40:1, reducing the required bore size and system pressure during clamping. All-electric machines use servo motor ball-screw drives for clamping in precision applications, but hydraulic machines retain dominance above 1,000 tons where electric servo systems cannot match hydraulic force density economically. Hybrid machines combine electric injection units with hydraulic clamp cylinders to capture speed and repeatability advantages while retaining hydraulic force capacity for high-tonnage requirements. The dependence on hydraulic clamping force remains a defining characteristic of full-hydraulic machines at every tonnage class from 5 tons to 4,000 tons. How Does a Tensile Testing Machine Use a Hydraulic System to Apply Force? A tensile testing machine uses a hydraulic system to apply precisely controlled tensile, compressive, or cyclic forces to a test specimen by converting hydraulic pressure into a calibrated load delivered through the crosshead and grips. The hydraulic actuator extends or retracts at programmable rates while a load cell measures applied force continuously from 0 to the machine's rated capacity. A servo-hydraulic testing machine connects a hydraulic power unit generating 3,000 psi to 5,000 psi to a precision servo valve that modulates actuator movement in response to electronic control signals. The servo valve adjusts fluid flow at update frequencies from 50 Hz to 1,000 Hz, enabling accurate testing across loading rates from quasi-static (0.001 inch per minute) to dynamic fatigue cycling at 100 Hz. Hydraulic testing machines reach force capacities from 10 kN to 2,000 kN, exceeding the range of electromechanical screw-drive machines without requiring proportionally larger motors. The actuator's force output remains consistent regardless of crosshead position or test speed, giving materials engineers a stable loading condition for evaluating tensile strength, yield strength, and elongation across metals, polymers, and composites tested on a Tensile Testing Machine . How Is Hydraulic Force Generated Inside a Tensile Testing Machine? Hydraulic force inside a tensile testing machine is generated when the power unit pressurizes the actuator cylinder, and the resulting pressure acting on the piston bore area produces a linear force transmitted through the crosshead to the specimen. Force follows F = P × A, where P is actuator pressure and A is effective piston area. A testing machine with a 4-inch bore actuator at 3,000 psi generates approximately 37,699 pounds (167.6 kN) of theoretical force, measured by the load cell after accounting for friction and seal resistance losses. The servo valve controls fluid flow direction and rate into the cylinder, determining crosshead travel direction and the rate at which load increases on the specimen. Closed-loop electronics compare the actual load cell signal to the commanded target at 50 Hz to 1,000 Hz update rates and adjust the servo valve to maintain target force within ±0.5% of the indicated load. The power unit maintains standby pressure at 500 psi to 1,000 psi from one test to the next, ensuring full actuator force is available within milliseconds of the next test command. Does a Tensile Testing Machine Use Hydraulic Pressure for Strength Testing? Yes, tensile testing machines use hydraulic pressure as the direct source of force for strength testing. The load cell measures actual specimen force independently of the hydraulic pressure reading, providing calibrated output traceable to ASTM E4 and ISO 7500-1 standards with accuracy of ±0.5% of indicated force. Hydraulic servo machines hold clear advantages over electromechanical alternatives in dynamic and fatigue testing. Cyclic tests requiring force amplitudes from ±1 kN to ±500 kN at 1 Hz to 100 Hz exceed the continuous capability of most screw-drive systems, while servo-hydraulic actuators sustain the required amplitude without thermal overload. Sinusoidal, triangular, trapezoidal, and random load spectra are achievable by modulating hydraulic pressure through the servo valve under computer control. Static tensile testing to ASTM E8, compressive testing of concrete to ASTM C39, and flexural testing all rely on consistent hydraulic force delivered at prescribed loading rates, confirming hydraulic pressure as the fundamental energy source for quantifying material strength across every standard test method. What Are Common Examples of Hydraulic Systems? The common examples of hydraulic systems are listed below. Excavators and Backhoes : Hydraulic excavators control the boom, arm, and bucket through circuits at 3,500 psi to 5,000 psi, generating bucket breakout forces from 10,000 to over 40,000 pounds. Swing motors, travel drives, and blade cylinders all operate from the same hydraulic power circuit. Automotive Braking Systems : Hydraulic disc brakes transmit pedal force through brake fluid to caliper pistons at line pressures from 300 psi to 1,500 psi, multiplying driver input by 20:1 to 40:1 through the master cylinder and booster. Aircraft Flight Control Systems : Commercial aircraft hydraulic systems at 3,000 psi to 5,000 psi actuate ailerons, elevators, rudders, flaps, and landing gear through redundant circuits that prevent total control loss from a single failure. Hydraulic Press Machines : Metal forming presses generate forces from 10 tons to 5,000 tons at 1,500 psi to 4,500 psi for blanking, deep drawing, and forging operations. Agricultural Equipment : Tractor three-point hitches and loader arms operate at 2,000 psi to 3,000 psi, lifting implements from 500 pounds to over 10,000 pounds with precise depth and draft control. Car lifts use hydraulic cylinders or scissor mechanisms to raise vehicles from 3,500 pounds to over 18,000 pounds, with two-post and four-post designs operating at 1,500 psi to 3,000 psi to reach lifting heights from 70 inches to 80 inches. Yes, hydraulic systems power the majority of construction and industrial equipment globally, and no equivalent technology has displaced hydraulic power transmission in high-force, mobile, or variable-load applications at comparable cost and reliability. A 500-ton hydraulic stamping press at 3,500 psi performs blanking and forming on steel sheet at 10 to 60 strokes per minute, producing forces no pneumatic actuator delivers at that scale without prohibitive cost. The dominance of hydraulic power in construction and industrial settings traces to four performance characteristics no alternative technology simultaneously matches: force density exceeding 1,000 horsepower per cubic foot of actuator volume, infinitely variable speed control from 0 to maximum, inherent overload protection through relief valves, and structural simplicity across a force range from 50 pounds to 5,000 tons. Electric and hybrid systems supplement hydraulic circuits in emissions-sensitive applications, but hydraulic power remains the primary force generation technology across every global market. events.after: Resources / Machining Design / How Does a Hydraulic System Work How Does a Hydraulic System Work Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 19 min read Published November 24, 2026 Updated November 25, 2026 A hydraulic system works by using pressurized fluid to transmit force from one point to another, enabling machines to perform heavy mechanical tasks with precision and control. The hydraulic system operates on Pascal's Law, which states that pressure applied to a confined fluid transmits equally in all directions, allowing a small input force to generate a significantly larger output force at the actuator. Hydraulic systems appear in excavators, aircraft landing gear, industrial presses, and injection molding machines because the fluid medium delivers a consistent, controllable force regardless of load orientation. Hydraulic systems are used in machines because they produce far greater force-to-size ratios than purely mechanical or pneumatic alternatives, with operating pressures commonly ranging from 1,000 psi to 5,000 psi in industrial equipment. The system type determines the application, with open-center, closed-center, and hydrostatic configurations each serving distinct operational requirements. A pump, reservoir, control valves, actuator, and hydraulic fluid form the core methodology through which energy converts into mechanical motion. The primary benefits include high power density, smooth speed control, overload protection through pressure relief valves, and the ability to transmit force over long distances without mechanical linkages. 1. Pump Pushes Fluid From Reservoir A hydraulic pump draws fluid from the reservoir and forces it into the system, converting mechanical energy into hydraulic flow. Gear, vane, and piston pumps generate flow rates from 1 GPM to over 100 GPM, depending on system size. Without continuous fluid displacement from the pump, no pressure builds, and no actuator movement occurs. 2. Input Force Creates Pressure Resistance encountered by the flowing fluid creates pressure within the system, measured in psi or bar. Pressure originates from the load or restriction opposing fluid flow at the actuator or control valve, not from the pump directly. A pump rated at 3,000 psi reaches that pressure only when the system load demands it. 3. Pressure Travels Through Fluid Pressurized fluid transmits force through hoses, tubes, and fittings with negligible energy loss over distance. Pascal's Law confirms that pressure applied at one point in a sealed fluid system transmits equally to every connected surface. Steel tubing rated to 6,000 psi and hydraulic hoses rated from 1,500 psi to 10,000 psi carry the pressurized fluid safely. 4. Fluid Reaches Actuator Directional control valves route pressurized fluid to the correct actuator port, determining whether the cylinder extends, retracts, or holds position. Fluid volume delivered to the actuator determines travel speed, while pressure determines the applied force. A closed-center valve locks the actuator in position when no command signal is present. 5. Actuator Produces Movement The actuator converts hydraulic pressure into mechanical force or motion through a cylinder or hydraulic motor. A double-acting cylinder with a 4-inch bore at 2,500 psi generates approximately 31,416 pounds of push force. Return fluid travels back to the reservoir after the stroke completes, finishing the closed-loop cycle. What Is a Hydraulic System? A hydraulic system is a power transmission technology that uses pressurized incompressible fluid to generate, control, and deliver mechanical force to actuators performing physical work. The system operates on Pascal's Law, established in 1647, confirming that pressure on a confined fluid transmits equally in all directions. Standard industrial hydraulic systems operate at 1,000 psi to 5,000 psi, with specialized systems reaching 10,000 psi to 15,000 psi in aerospace applications. The fluid serves simultaneously as the power carrier, lubricant, and heat transfer agent, distinguishing hydraulic systems from mechanical or pneumatic alternatives. Petroleum-based hydraulic oil with viscosity grades from ISO VG 32 to ISO VG 68 fills the reservoir, pump, valve block, and actuator circuit continuously during operation. Force multiplication through piston area ratios makes it possible to lift loads exceeding 50 tons using a compact pump driven by a 50-horsepower motor. Hydraulic systems serve aerospace, construction, manufacturing, agriculture, and marine industries because no equivalent technology delivers the same combination of force density, controllability, and design flexibility. What Are the Main Components of a Hydraulic System? The main components of a hydraulic system are listed below. Hydraulic Reservoir : The reservoir stores hydraulic fluid from 5 gallons to over 500 gallons, dissipates heat from returning fluid, and provides a steady supply to the pump inlet without cavitation. Hydraulic Pump : The pump converts mechanical energy into hydraulic flow, with gear, vane, and piston pumps covering flow ranges from 1 GPM to 150 GPM at pressures from 1,500 psi to 6,000 psi. Control Valves : Directional, pressure relief, and flow control valves manage fluid routing, maximum operating pressure, and actuator speed. Pressure relief valves are set from 500 psi to 5,000 psi to prevent system overpressure. Actuators : Hydraulic cylinders and motors convert fluid pressure into mechanical force or torque. A cylinder with a 3-inch bore at 2,000 psi generates approximately 14,137 pounds of linear force. Hydraulic Fluid : Petroleum-based or synthetic fluid transmits pressure while lubricating internal surfaces. ISO VG 46 is the most commonly specified viscosity grade for industrial systems operating at 40°C to 80°C. Filters and Seals : Filters rated at 3 to 25 microns remove particulate contamination, while seals prevent leakage at pressures up to 6,000 psi. Is the Pump Responsible for Creating Flow in the System? Yes, the pump creates flow in a hydraulic system, but it does not directly create pressure. The pump displaces a fixed or variable volume of fluid per revolution, establishing a flow rate in GPM. Pressure develops only in response to the resistance the flowing fluid encounters at the load, actuator, or closed valve. A gear pump at 1,800 RPM with 0.5 cubic inches per revolution displacement delivers approximately 3.9 GPM regardless of system pressure. Increasing pump speed raises flow and actuator speed, while increasing system load raises pressure without changing pump flow rate. Variable displacement piston pumps adjust output volume automatically in response to system demand, reducing flow to near zero when the actuator reaches full extension and maintaining standby pressure from 200 psi to 500 psi without energy waste. The pump originates all fluid movement in the circuit, and load resistance downstream transforms that movement into working pressure that performs mechanical work. Why Are Hydraulic Systems Used in Machines? Hydraulic systems are used in machines because they deliver exceptionally high force output relative to component size, a characteristic no purely mechanical or electromechanical system matches at equivalent scale. A hydraulic cylinder with a 6-inch bore at 3,000 psi produces over 84,823 pounds of force from a unit weighing under 50 pounds. Machines rely on hydraulic systems for precise, stepless speed and force control across variable output ranges. A proportional flow control valve adjusts actuator speed continuously from 0 to maximum, giving operators exact positioning authority over loads exceeding several tons without discrete steps or complex mechanical transmissions. Hydraulic systems also provide inherent overload protection through pressure relief valves preset from 1,500 psi to 5,000 psi, redirecting excess fluid to the reservoir automatically when an overload occurs. No operator intervention is required to protect downstream components. The combination of high force density, smooth controllability, and overload protection explains why construction excavators, aircraft control surfaces, industrial presses, and agricultural equipment all depend on hydraulic power as a core engineering solution. How Do Hydraulic Machines Multiply Force? Hydraulic machines multiply force by applying pressure across different piston surface areas within the same sealed circuit, following Pascal's Law, where Force equals Pressure multiplied by Area (F = P × A). A small pump piston generating 2,000 psi transmits that exact pressure to a large actuator cylinder, where the greater surface area produces a proportionally larger output force. A pump piston with a 1-square-inch area receiving 100 pounds of input generates 100 psi system pressure. Acting on a cylinder bore with a 20-square-inch area, the same 100 psi produces 2,000 pounds of output force, a 20-to-1 multiplication ratio. The trade-off is travel distance: the large cylinder moves a shorter distance than the input piston for the same fluid volume displaced. Hydraulic press systems in metal stamping exploit the multiplication principle at an industrial scale, with cylinder bore diameters reaching 24 inches at 3,000 psi to generate forces exceeding 1,000 tons. The force multiplication ratio scales directly with the actuator-to-pump piston area ratio across every application size. Are Hydraulic Systems More Powerful Than Mechanical Systems of the Same Size? Yes, hydraulic systems are more powerful than mechanical systems of the same physical size. A hydraulic motor delivering 50 horsepower occupies approximately one-third the volume and one-fourth the weight of a mechanical gearbox transmitting equivalent power at the same output torque. Hydraulic actuators achieve force levels of tens of thousands of pounds from cylinders compact enough to fit inside a vehicle chassis or aircraft wing, where no mechanical alternative packages equally. Energy travels at pressures from 1,000 psi to 5,000 psi through hoses and compact valves, eliminating the rigid shafts, gears, and bearings that add mass to mechanical power trains. Mechanical systems maintain efficiency advantages in steady-state transmission, with spur gear drives reaching 95% to 99% efficiency compared to 70% to 85% for hydraulic systems due to fluid friction and internal leakage losses. The efficiency gap narrows in variable-speed applications where hydraulic systems avoid throttling losses of fixed-ratio mechanical drives, confirming that power density and application context together determine which technology performs better at a given size. Why Are Hydraulic Fluids Important in Hydraulic Systems? Hydraulic fluids are important because the fluid simultaneously serves as the energy transmission medium, internal lubricant, heat transfer agent, and sealant across the entire operating cycle. No other single element performs as many simultaneous functions, making fluid selection and condition directly responsible for system performance and component service life. The fluid transmits pressure with minimal compressibility, quantified by a bulk modulus ranging from 200,000 psi to 300,000 psi for petroleum-based hydraulic oils. The high bulk modulus ensures pressure changes at the pump translate immediately into actuator force without energy absorption lag. The fluid also lubricates pump gears, valve spools, and cylinder surfaces, with viscosity maintained from ISO VG 32 to ISO VG 68 at operating temperatures from 40°C to 80°C. Heat generated by pressure drops across valves and pump friction accumulates in the fluid, which carries thermal energy to the reservoir and heat exchanger for dissipation. Contaminated or degraded Hydraulic Fluids account for 70% to 80% of all hydraulic system failures, confirming that fluid condition governs overall system reliability more than any other maintenance variable. How Do Hydraulic Fluids Transfer Power in Industrial Machines? Hydraulic fluids transfer power in industrial machines by acting as an incompressible medium that carries pressure energy from the pump through the valve circuit to the actuator with minimal energy loss. The fluid fills the entire enclosed circuit continuously, meaning pressure generated at the pump reaches the cylinder or motor in milliseconds, regardless of circuit distance. Power transfer efficiency depends on fluid viscosity at operating temperature. Viscosity too low allows internal leakage across pump and valve clearances of 0.001 inch to 0.003 inch, dropping volumetric efficiency below 90% and wasting output as heat. Viscosity too high increases flow resistance and pressure drop across valve passages. ISO VG 46 at 50°C maintains approximately 46 centistokes, balancing leakage control with acceptable flow resistance in most industrial applications. Additive packages in industrial fluids improve transfer reliability by preventing oxidation, foam, and surface wear. Anti-wear additives containing zinc dialkyldithiophosphate (ZDDP) protect pump pistons and valve lands operating under contact pressures from 50,000 psi to 200,000 psi, maintaining the dimensional precision that volumetric efficiency requires throughout the service interval. Are Hydraulic Fluids Essential for Pressure and Lubrication Control? Yes, hydraulic fluids are essential for pressure control and lubrication, and neither function operates independently. The same fluid transmitting working pressure from 1,000 psi to 5,000 psi simultaneously lubricates every internal moving surface it contacts within the pump, valves, and actuator. Pressure control depends on fluid incompressibility. Petroleum-based hydraulic oil compresses less than 0.5% per 1,000 psi of applied pressure, making it an effective transmission medium that responds to load changes without absorbing significant energy. Degraded fluid with a reduced bulk modulus slows pressure response and decreases actuator positioning accuracy measurably. Lubrication control depends on maintaining adequate viscosity at operating temperature. Pump pistons, shoes, and swash plates rely on a hydrodynamic fluid film of 1 to 10 micrometers to prevent metal-to-metal contact at relative surface velocities from 1 to 10 meters per second. Allowing fluid viscosity to drop below 10 centistokes at maximum operating temperature collapses the film and reduces pump service life from 10,000 hours to below 2,000 hours. Plastic injection molding machines use hydraulic systems to generate and control the forces required for mold clamping, plastic injection, pack hold, and part ejection, with each phase demanding precise force and speed control at production cycle times of seconds per shot. The clamping unit uses large-bore hydraulic cylinders with bore diameters from 8 inches to 24 inches to hold mold halves closed against injection pressure. A mold with a 100-square-inch projected area at 15,000 psi injection pressure requires at least 750 tons of clamping force to prevent flash formation at the parting line. The hydraulic clamp cylinder generates equivalent force at system pressures from 2,000 psi to 3,500 psi through piston area advantage. The injection unit drives the screw forward at velocities from 50 mm per second to 500 mm per second, forcing molten polymer through runners and gates at fill pressures from 10,000 psi to 30,000 psi. Proportional hydraulic valves control injection speed and holding pressure independently during each phase, giving process engineers the precision needed to maintain dimensional tolerances in Plastic Injection Molding Machines producing parts to ±0.001-inch specifications. Why Is Hydraulic Pressure Critical in Plastic Injection Molding Machines? Hydraulic pressure is critical in plastic injection molding machines because every phase of the cycle requires a distinct pressure level, and the hydraulic system must switch from one to another within milliseconds to maintain part quality and dimensional consistency. Hydraulic pressure from 2,000 psi to 3,500 psi must exceed the separating force generated by melt pressure inside the cavity during clamping. Insufficient clamp pressure causes flash defects at the parting line, while excess pressure accelerates mold wear. During injection, hydraulic pressure drives fill at 10,000 psi to 30,000 psi and then maintains pack pressure from 5,000 psi to 15,000 psi to compensate for polymer shrinkage during cooling. Pack pressure directly controls part weight, sink mark depth, and dimensional stability. A 5% variation in pack pressure produces measurable changes in part mass and feature dimensions for precision components (medical device housings and optical lenses). Pressure consistency across thousands of cycles, maintained by closed-loop hydraulic control, determines whether the machine produces parts within specification across high-volume production runs. Do Plastic Injection Molding Machines Rely on Hydraulic Force for Clamping? Yes, plastic injection hydraulic molding machines rely on hydraulic force for clamping, with clamp cylinders generating forces from 5 tons to over 4,000 tons through direct-acting or toggle-assisted hydraulic arrangements. A direct hydraulic clamp uses a single large-bore cylinder behind the moving platen to generate clamping force directly from hydraulic pressure. A toggle clamp uses a hydraulic cylinder to actuate a mechanical linkage that multiplies cylinder force by a ratio of 20:1 to 40:1, reducing the required bore size and system pressure during clamping. All-electric machines use servo motor ball-screw drives for clamping in precision applications, but hydraulic machines retain dominance above 1,000 tons where electric servo systems cannot match hydraulic force density economically. Hybrid machines combine electric injection units with hydraulic clamp cylinders to capture speed and repeatability advantages while retaining hydraulic force capacity for high-tonnage requirements. The dependence on hydraulic clamping force remains a defining characteristic of full-hydraulic machines at every tonnage class from 5 tons to 4,000 tons. A tensile testing machine uses a hydraulic system to apply precisely controlled tensile, compressive, or cyclic forces to a test specimen by converting hydraulic pressure into a calibrated load delivered through the crosshead and grips. The hydraulic actuator extends or retracts at programmable rates while a load cell measures applied force continuously from 0 to the machine's rated capacity. The power unit maintains standby pressure at 500 psi to 1,000 psi from one test to the next, ensuring full actuator force is available within milliseconds of the next test command. events.before: Resources / Machining Design / How Laser Engraving Aluminum Works How Laser Engraving Aluminum Works Written by Joel Schadegg 7 min read Published February 25, 2022 Updated November 20, 2026 Learn more about laser engraving aluminum in our in-depth guide Laser engraving involves making deep permanent marks on a metal surface. The incision occurs by focusing a laser beam onto the metal surface in a specified pattern, thus removing some materials through vaporization. Aluminum is a versatile material that’s become indispensable in most industries for its durability, exceptional corrosion resistance, and lightweight properties. It offers limitless design possibilities thanks to its numerous processing options. Thanks to this, it has found use in a range of industries including the aerospace, automotive, electronics, building, and construction fields, among others. Laser engraving in aluminum is an important part marking process as it embeds permanent codes on components for easy traceability. Read on to discover how laser engraving in aluminum works, its pros and cons, and some tips to design for laser engraved aluminum part marking. If you’re looking to learn more about other types of marking, you can also check out our guide on direct and other part markings . Xometry parts displaying laser engraving How Laser Engraving Works with Aluminum A powerful beam acts as the chisel in aluminum laser engraving, vaporizing particles off the metal surface to incise deep marks. The laser engraver should radiate enough energy that the beam excites the surface material to its vaporization temperature, which for aluminum is 4,221 degrees F, or 2,327 degrees C. Vaporization happens within seconds to avoid generating liquid residue. Modern laser marking systems feature a fume extraction mechanism and an air knife. Fume extraction prevents the release of harmful fumes into the work environment, while the air knife safeguards the laser’s lens. Types of engraving lasers There are two types of lasers used in aluminum engraving: fiber laser systems and CO2 lasers. Fiber lasers operate at a wavelength that reacts better with metals. They are efficient in creating a high-contrast, durable mark without interfering with the integrity of the parts. They are also long-lasting and come at a lower price. This makes them common for industrial part marking applications. CO2 laser engraving of aluminum is also possible; these lasers can also be applied to non-metallic parts made from acrylics, woods, and natural stone, so they are more commonly used by manufacturers that handle a wider range of materials. Laser marking systems are controlled through computer software. Aluminum laser markings remain on the surface permanently. This is important for aluminum specifically because workpieces from this material are exposed to numerous kinds of wear and surface treatments. Engravings do not wear out, tear, degrade, or get discarded no matter how long the component lasts or the processes it undergoes. That makes it a suitable marking process for parts that may undergo further rigorous treatments in the manufacturing process such as sandblasting and shot blasting. Laser etching aluminum can also be more beneficial to the environment than other marking methods if a suitable machine is used. Why use laser engraving for part marking? Aluminum laser incising is the perfect technology for engraving marks on parts made of this metal. This is because aluminum workpieces are exposed to numerous kinds of wear and surface treatments. Marks made through this process remain on the surfaces forever. They do not wear out, tear, degrade, or get discarded no matter how long the component lasts or the processes it undergoes. That makes it a suitable marking process for parts that may undergo rigorous treatments such as sandblasting and shot blasting. Besides, by choosing to laser etch aluminum, industries ensure they don’t expose any harm to the environment as long as they use a suitable machine. Also, the engraving machine can do so many different tasks for the owner's benefit. Why is part marking done? Why mark parts? As mentioned earlier, part marking enables accurate tracking of the serial number of a component through a marked QR code, data matrix code, or serial numbers. It’s also helpful in part identification and tracking statistics in component manufacturing and application. Part marking is thus vital for quality control and supply chain functions. Other reasons for part marking include: To differentiate parts that look similar To facilitate part assembly To link the part or product to the company and machine on which it was produced For simple labeling Laser Engraving Bare Aluminum vs. Anodized Aluminum Both bare and anodized aluminum can be engraved with fiber laser, though it can be more challenging to engrave bare aluminum with a CO2 laser than anodized aluminum. The best system for engraving bare aluminum sheet metals is a fiber laser. For CO2 lasers, the operator must spray a special paste as a pretreatment for the metal. Then, the CO2 laser produces heat that glues the chiseling agent to the bare aluminum. The process takes time and calls for high power configuration. If not done at a low speed and with high power settings, the marks can easily wipe off, thus requiring a repeat job. Because of these factors, it can cost more to have a CO2 laser perform the same process. However, no material is removed with a CO2 laser marking, so the marking doesn’t affect the material’s integrity. Anodized aluminum, however, can be engraved with equal ease using either type of laser. Anodized aluminum is simply aluminum with an oxide layer coating. This coating makes the material more corrosion and UV resistant while offering better lubrication and low-cost maintenance. events.before: Resources / Machining Design / How Does Metal Engraving Work? How Does Metal Engraving Work? Written by Greg Paulsen Updated by Aaron Lichtig 6 min read Published February 22, 2022 Updated November 20, 2026 Engraving was a historically important means of producing images on paper in artistic printmaking, mapmaking, and commercial reproductions and illustrations for the publishing industry. Various photographic processes have long replaced it in its commercial applications and, partly because of its complexity, is much less common in printmaking and has been largely replaced by etching and other techniques. However, engraving is still common in other industries. Metal engraving is used to mark text, logos, pictures, numbers, 2D codes, and more. The industries that engrave metal include jewelry, medical, automotive, aeronautics, and energy, to name a few. Engraving is the process of creating letters, lines, or designs by incising surfaces. Engraving can be used on a variety of materials such as glass, plastic, and stone, but this article will focus on metals. laser engraved parts by Xometry Metal Engraving Methods The following methods are common processes performed in most engraving shops. Diamond-Drag Scratch Engraving This process uses a non-rotating tool with a cone-shaped diamond tip. The engraving tool is dragged through the metal part, leaving an impression. Diamond-drag creates quality and precise engraving that compares to hand engraving. The width of the stroke is constant and does not vary in depth. Diamond drag is recommended for soft metals and is ideal for engraving jewelry and trophies. The benefits of this method are that it is generally the fastest form of engraving, is the least expensive, and the width of the stroke allows for small engraved letters. One drawback is that it has a limited stroke width. Burnishing Burnishing uses a rotating tool with limited pressure. The tool is either carbide or a diamond cutter of varying tip width that removes the top coating or layer of material and creates a smooth, polished finish. Burnishing can stand in for situations where diamond drag is used. Burnishing is still a newer process for many shops. The benefits of burnishing are the virtually unlimited stroke width and the larger letter heights that can be achieved. Some drawbacks are that it is more expensive and requires a noisy engraving motor and an additional burnishing adapter. Rotary Engraving This method uses a single or multiple fluted cutting tool that rotates through metal parts to remove material, leaving a trough of the exposed core. It results in a deeper cut or the complete cut-out of a letter or object. In most applications, the spindle micrometer setting controls the depth of the cut. The process is suitable for most commercial and industrial work. Rotary engraving is the most permanent form of engraving and allows virtually any size of letter to be created, and can achieve two- and three-dimensional appearances. Some drawbacks are that it requires a broader selection of cutting tools, a rotary spindle, and a motor, and generally requires more clean-up. Laser Beam Engraving A laser engraver can cut, engrave, or mark metal materials. The laser beam physically removes the metal’s surface to create a cavity that reveals an image at eye level. The laser beam produces high heat during the process, which essentially causes the substance to vaporize. The benefits of laser engraving are that it allows for more detailed images, cleaner cuts, it’s faster, it’s fairly affordable, and it doesn’t create waste such as sawdust. The drawbacks are that thicker materials are more difficult for laser cutting or require very low speeds, and the laser burns the edges of any material being cut. A laser engraving machine can also use a lot of energy, increasing the production cost. Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo Engraved Metals Some of the most commonly engraved metals are: Aluminum Brightly coated or anodized aluminum is used to make plaques or trophy plates. Machining grade aluminum is used to construct control panels, interior and exterior signage, and industrial applications. Its surface can be temperamental compared to brass, copper, and bronze. However, almost all aluminum alloys will cut with some experimentation and patience. Brass Commercially purchased brass is hard to engrave. “Engravers Brass” or “half-hard” brass is much softer and can be found at engraving material suppliers. For deep cut signage, brass with a thickness of .040-.060 in. is recommended. This metal can be paint-filled for contrast between the letters and the brass background. Laser etching brass creates a bold black mark on the metal alloy, making it a very commonly marked metal. Stainless Steel Stainless steel is harder to engrave but has many benefits. It is very durable, corrosion-resistant, moisture-resistant, and doesn't contaminate other materials. It is used in food processing plants and hospitals where a reaction or corrosion would destroy most metals. Its other applications include containers, control panels, switch and legend plates, signs, and elevator panels. When cutting stainless steel, a collet spindle is one of the most important tools. The collet spindle with a split collet grabs the cutting tool vary close to the work area. This extra rigidity will allow for deeper cuts and less cutter chipping or breaking. Laser engraving cannot be used on steel as the heat from the laser removes an important protective layer, but laser annealing can. Gold, Silver, Pewter These metals are soft and are easily cut. They work well for gift items in most engraving applications, such as jewelry personalization, and diamond drag engraving is the method of choice. These materials can be deep cut easily with the same cutting tools used for brass. In most cases, no cutting fluids are necessary. The Difference Between Metal Laser Engraving and Laser Marking Laser marking uses a focused laser beam to alter the surface of the workpiece permanently. Unlike laser engraving, it changes the metal’s surface without removing material. As a result, it creates long-lasting high-contrast marks that can easily be read or scanned. The four most commonly used laser marking methods are annealing, carbon migration, coloring, and foaming. A metal marking compound is sometimes applied before laser marking to allow easier marking and higher contrast mark. Fiber or galvanometer laser systems are typically used to mark bare metals and engineered plastics. These lasers have different wavelengths than CO2 lasers, which allow them to mark bare metals without using metal marking agents. While laser marking and laser engraving are terms often used interchangeably as laser processes, they differ. As explained above, laser engraving is a manufacturing process that uses a laser beam to remove material from the metal to form the desired design. The results are durable and resistant to falsification. The three most common laser cutting techniques are laser etching, laser engraving, and laser ablation. The main difference between etching and engraving and ablation is that laser etching produces shallow marks, while laser engraving creates deep marks that are more durable. Summary Metal engraving techniques are useful to provide for permanent part marking and tagging of products across different industries. events.before: Resources / Machining Design / Least Material Condition (LMC): Tolerance Control, Minimum Material Limits, and Design Applications Least Material Condition (LMC): Tolerance Control, Minimum Material Limits, and Design Applications Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 21 min read Published July 16, 2026 Updated November 20, 2026 The least material condition refers to the dimensional state of a feature when it holds the smallest permissible amount of material within its defined tolerance range. The least material condition governs minimum wall thickness in Geometric Dimensioning and Tolerancing (GD&T), edge distance, and structural integrity, allowing controlled geometric variation within defined size limits. Engineers apply it across aerospace structures, thin-wall components, pressure systems, and precision machining environments where material retention directly affects part performance. The standard, defined in ASME Y14.5, governs how features behave at their dimensional extremes without compromising structural function. Understanding the least material condition requires distinguishing it from the Maximum Material Condition (MMC) and from the Regardless of Feature Size (RFS) modifier, as each modifier controls tolerance behavior differently. LMC specifically addresses the minimum material state, making it the preferred control for features where insufficient material leads to failure. In aerospace manufacturing, pressure system components and precision-machined housings, applying the correct material condition modifier prevents structural weakness at the feature level. The Ⓛ symbol in a feature control frame signals that geometric tolerance is evaluated at the least material condition (LMC), with additional tolerance permitted as the feature departs toward MMC. What Is the Least Material Condition (LMC)? The Least Material Condition (LMC) is the condition where a feature contains the minimum material allowed by its dimensional tolerance limits. ASME-based GD&T defines LMC as the least material state of a feature of size, which protects the minimum material around critical geometry. A hole reaches LMC at its largest allowable diameter, since the larger opening removes material from the part. A shaft reaches LMC at its smallest allowable diameter, since the smaller outside size leaves less material in the feature. LMC matters in engineering drawings where the minimum wall thickness, edge distance, and remaining strength control the part function. Aerospace brackets, pressure ports, thin-wall housings, and machined structural plates use LMC when excessive material removal weakens a feature. GD&T applies the circled L symbol to show that a geometric tolerance relates to the least material limit.
