Cast iron grades differ based on composition, microstructure, and mechanical properties. The form of carbon present in the alloy, whether as graphite flakes, nodules, or carbides, defines the grade classification. The carbon content in cast iron ranges from 2% to 4%, and the way carbon is distributed across the matrix determines the material's behavior under load. Variations in alloying elements such as silicon (1% to 3%), manganese (0.2% to 1%), sulfur, and phosphorus further separate one grade from another. Silicon, for instance, promotes graphite formation, while manganese stabilizes the iron carbide phase. The microstructure resulting from the combination of carbon form and alloying elements dictates whether the material exhibits brittle fracture or moderate flexibility. For example, Gray cast iron contains lamellar graphite flakes that act as stress concentrators, reducing tensile strength to a range from 100 MPa to 370 MPa. Ductile cast iron contains spherical graphite nodules, raising tensile strength to a range from 400 MPa to 900 MPa. The grade system communicates precise mechanical thresholds, allowing engineers to match material performance to structural demands. What Do Cast Iron Grades Indicate About Strength and Hardness? Cast iron grades indicate the level of strength and hardness a material delivers under specific loading and environmental conditions. Each grade corresponds to measurable mechanical values, including tensile strength in megapascals, Brinell hardness numbers (BHN), and yield strength thresholds. Gray iron grades, classified under ASTM A48, range from Class 20 to Class 60, where the number directly reflects the minimum tensile strength in ksi (kilopounds per square inch). A Class 20 gray iron has a tensile strength of 20 ksi, while a Class 60 delivers 60 ksi. Higher grades reflect improved mechanical performance through refined microstructures and controlled alloy additions. Ductile iron grades under ASTM A536, for example, include Grade 60-40-18, Grade 80-55-06, and Grade 120-90-02, where the first number represents tensile strength, the second represents yield strength, and the third represents percent elongation. The hardness values for gray cast iron range from 150 BHN to 320 BHN, depending on grade, while ductile iron ranges from 140 BHN to 300 BHN. The grades guide material selection by providing engineers with standardized performance benchmarks, helping match the right cast iron type to specific structural, thermal, or wear-resistance requirements. Are Higher Grades Associated With Better Mechanical Properties? Yes, higher grades are associated with better mechanical properties. Higher-grade cast irons exhibit greater tensile strength, increased yield strength, and improved resistance to deformation under load. The refined graphite morphology and heat treatment processes applied to higher grades reduce internal stress concentrations, increasing resistance to fatigue and impact. Higher-grade gray iron, classified as Class 40 or Class 60 under ASTM A48, achieves a finer pearlitic matrix, which contributes to greater surface hardness and wear resistance. The performance advantage of higher-grade cast iron becomes evident in heavy-duty applications (engine components, hydraulic housings, and structural machine bases), where consistent mechanical behavior under cyclic stress is required. The superior load performance of higher grades confirms their role in demanding industrial environments. What Is the Role of Iron in Cast Iron Types? The role of iron in cast iron types acts as the base element in all cast iron types, forming the primary structural matrix that supports and interacts with carbon and other alloying elements. Cast iron is an iron-carbon alloy where the iron content ranges from 92% to 96% by weight, making it the dominant phase in the material's composition. The crystalline structure of the iron matrix, whether ferritic, pearlitic, or martensitic, determines the mechanical behavior of the final casting. A ferritic matrix promotes ductility, while a pearlitic matrix increases hardness and strength. The iron phase acts as the host structure into which carbon precipitates during solidification. Depending on cooling rate and silicon content, carbon either forms graphite or iron carbide (Fe₃C) within the iron matrix. The properties of cast iron are modified by alloying elements such as carbon, silicon, manganese, sulfur, and phosphorus, while Iron (Fe) remains the main structural component of the material. The iron matrix determines core properties, including compressive strength, thermal conductivity, and machinability. Gray cast iron, which contains a predominantly pearlitic iron matrix, achieves a compressive strength ranging from 570 MPa to 1,380 MPa, a value driven by the iron phase. Silicon content ranging from 1% to 3% directly controls how the iron matrix responds to carbon, either stabilizing graphite formation or promoting carbide formation. Additives (chromium, nickel, and molybdenum) modify the iron matrix by stabilizing specific crystalline phases, changing hardness and wear resistance. The base iron phase remains unchanged in composition regardless of additive content, maintaining its role as the structural foundation across all cast iron types. The iron-carbon system at high carbon concentrations defines the eutectic point at 4.3% carbon and 1,147°C, which governs the solidification behavior and final microstructure of the cast iron product. Yes, cast iron is more brittle than steel. The higher carbon content in cast iron, ranging from 2% to 4%, leads to the formation of graphite phases or iron carbide (cementite) within the microstructure, both of which reduce the material's capacity for plastic deformation. Steel contains carbon from 0.02% to 2.1%, which remains dissolved within the iron matrix as a solid solution or fine carbide precipitates, allowing for significantly greater ductility and toughness. The elongation at break for gray cast iron is near 0%, while structural steels (ASTM A36) achieve elongation values from 20% to 23%. The fracture toughness of gray cast iron ranges from 10 MPa√m to 15 MPa√m, while medium-carbon steels reach from 40 MPa√m to 100 MPa√m. The brittle behavior of cast iron makes it susceptible to sudden fracture under impact or tensile loading without prior visible deformation. Steel deforms plastically before fracture, giving engineers a warning before structural failure occurs. Ductile iron reduces the brittleness gap with steel by converting graphite to nodular form, achieving elongation from 2% to 18%, though it still falls short of the ductility values exhibited by most structural steels. The higher carbon phase content in cast iron is the primary reason for the brittleness difference from steel. What Are Different Types of Cast Iron Used? The different types of cast iron used are listed below. Gray Cast Iron: Gray cast iron is used in applications requiring high compressive strength, vibration damping, and good machinability. Engine blocks, machine tool bases, and brake rotors rely on the graphite flake network to absorb and dissipate vibrations and heat. The thermal conductivity value from 46 W/m·K to 51 W/m·K makes it effective in heat transfer components (cookware and furnace parts). Ductile Cast Iron: Ductile cast iron is used in structural and dynamic load applications where tensile strength and impact resistance are required. Pipes, gears, crankshafts, and automotive suspension components rely on the nodular graphite structure for fatigue resistance and flexibility. The tensile strength from 400 MPa to 900 MPa supports high-load mechanical assemblies. White Cast Iron: White cast iron is used in extreme wear environments where hardness from 400 HB to 700 HB is the primary requirement. Wear-resistant liners, grinding balls, and mill plates in mineral processing equipment are made of white cast iron. The high carbide content provides abrasion resistance but limits use in impact-heavy environments due to brittleness. Malleable Cast Iron: Malleable cast iron is used in applications requiring moderate ductility and machinability in complex shapes. Pipe fittings, brackets, and hand tools are produced from malleable cast iron due to its capacity for controlled deformation and precise casting geometries. The elongation from 5% to 12% allows it to absorb mechanical stress without fracturing. Compacted Graphite Iron (CGI): CGI is used in high-performance diesel engine blocks and exhaust manifolds where thermal fatigue resistance and strength from 300 MPa to 500 MPa are required. The vermicular graphite structure delivers thermal conductivity near 38 W/m·K to 45 W/m·K, superior to ductile iron for heat dissipation. CGI reduces engine block weight while maintaining structural integrity under high cylinder pressures. Alloy Cast Iron: Alloy cast iron is used in heat-resistant, corrosion-resistant, and wear-resistant components across chemical processing, pumping systems, and high-temperature industrial equipment. Nickel-alloyed cast irons resist oxidation at temperatures up to 900°C, while chromium-alloyed variants achieve hardness up to 800 HB for abrasion-resistant applications. Pumps handling corrosive fluids, heat exchanger components, and furnace grates rely on alloy cast iron grades for long service life. 1. Gray Cast Iron Used for Engine Blocks, Machine Bases, and Brake Rotors Gray cast iron is the most widely produced cast iron type, accounting for approximately 70% to 75% of total cast iron production globally. The graphite flake microstructure provides a compressive strength from 570 MPa to 1,380 MPa, making it well-suited for engine blocks that experience high cylinder pressures. Machine bases and lathe beds use gray cast iron for its vibration-damping capacity, which reduces tool chatter and improves dimensional accuracy during machining operations. Brake rotors rely on the thermal conductivity from 46 W/m·K to 51 W/m·K to dissipate frictional heat generated during repeated braking cycles, preventing thermal distortion. The Brinell hardness of gray cast iron ranges from 150 HB to 320 HB, providing adequate surface wear resistance for brake rotor contact faces. The graphite flakes act as a built-in lubricant during machining, reducing cutting forces and extending tool life in high-volume manufacturing environments. 2. Ductile Cast Iron Used for Pipes, Gears, Crankshafts, and Automotive Components Ductile cast iron is used across piping infrastructure, power transmission components, and automotive drivetrains due to its tensile strength from 400 MPa to 900 MPa and elongation from 2% to 18%. Ductile iron pipes used in water distribution systems conform to ISO 2531 and AWWA C151 standards, with pressure ratings from 16 bar to 100 bar, depending on wall thickness and diameter. Crankshafts manufactured from Grade 80-55-06 ductile iron achieve yield strengths of 55 ksi, providing fatigue resistance under cyclic bending and torsional loads from engine operation. Gears made from ductile iron benefit from the nodular graphite structure, which distributes contact stresses evenly across gear teeth, reducing pitting and spalling wear. Automotive suspension components (steering knuckles and control arms) use ductile iron to absorb road impact loads without brittle fracture, offering a cost-effective alternative to forged steel in high-volume vehicle production. 3. White Cast Iron Used for Wear-Resistant Liners, Grinding Balls, and Mill Plates White cast iron is used exclusively in high-abrasion environments due to its hardness from 400 HB to 700 HB, derived from the iron carbide (cementite, Fe₃C) phase that forms throughout the microstructure. Wear-resistant liners in ball mills and rod mills protect the shell from ore and mineral abrasion, with white cast iron liners lasting significantly longer than mild steel in comparable grinding environments. Grinding balls used in cement and mineral processing plants are produced from high-chrome white cast iron containing 12% to 28% chromium, which forms M₇C₃ carbides with hardness from 1,200 HV to 1,600 HV. Mill plates in crushing and grinding equipment rely on the continuous carbide network to resist metal loss under sustained abrasive contact with hard minerals. The brittleness of white cast iron limits its use to compressive and sliding wear conditions, where tensile and impact loads remain low during operation. 4. Malleable Cast Iron Used for Pipe Fittings, Brackets, and Hand Tools Malleable cast iron is produced by annealing white cast iron at temperatures from 900°C to 970°C for periods from 20 to 70 hours, converting brittle cementite into temper carbon clusters within a ferritic or pearlitic matrix. The resulting tensile strength from 275 MPa to 550 MPa and elongation from 5% to 12% allow malleable cast iron to handle mechanical stress without fracturing at stress concentrations. Pipe fittings manufactured from malleable cast iron conform to ASTM A197 and ASTM A220 standards, where the material's machinability and thread-cutting performance support precision thread profiles. Brackets and structural connectors use malleable cast iron for its ability to be cast into complex geometries that require thin sections and sharp internal corners. Hand tools (wrenches, clamps, and vise bodies) rely on malleable cast iron for moderate impact resistance and the ability to deform slightly before fracturing, improving safety in field applications. 5. Compacted Graphite Iron Used for Diesel Engine Blocks and Exhaust Manifolds Compacted graphite iron is used in diesel engine blocks and exhaust manifolds because it delivers a combination of thermal conductivity from 38 W/m·K to 45 W/m·K, tensile strength from 300 MPa to 500 MPa, and fatigue resistance superior to gray cast iron. Diesel engine blocks manufactured from CGI allow cylinder bore pressures exceeding 200 bar without structural failure, meeting the demands of modern high-performance compression ignition engines. The vermicular graphite structure provides 75% greater tensile strength and 45% greater stiffness than gray cast iron, reducing the need for additional wall thickness and lowering component weight. Exhaust manifolds fabricated from CGI withstand thermal cycling from ambient temperatures to over 700°C without cracking, a critical requirement for turbocharged diesel applications. The material's fatigue strength from 200 MPa to 280 MPa supports the repeated pressure pulses generated during multi-cylinder diesel engine operation at high load conditions. 6. Alloy Cast Iron Used for Heat-Resistant Parts, Pumps, and Corrosion-Resistant Components Alloy cast iron incorporates elements (nickel, chromium, molybdenum, and copper) to extend the performance of base cast iron into high-temperature, corrosive, and extreme-wear environments. Nickel-alloyed cast irons (Ni-Resist grades) containing 14% to 36% nickel resist oxidation and scaling at temperatures from 800°C to 1,050°C, making them suitable for furnace grates, kiln furniture, and heat treatment fixtures. Chromium-alloyed white cast irons containing 12% to 28% chromium achieve hardness from 550 HB to 800 HB, used in pump impellers and volute casings handling abrasive slurries in mining and mineral processing. Molybdenum additions from 0.25% to 1% increase hardenability and improve high-temperature creep resistance in alloy cast iron components exposed to sustained thermal loads. Corrosion-resistant alloy cast irons containing silicon from 14% to 17% (high-silicon grades) resist concentrated sulfuric acid and nitric acid, making them the preferred material for chemical processing pump bodies and valve housings. What Are the Advantages of Using Different Types of Cast Iron? The advantages of using different types of Cast Iron are listed below. Gray Cast Iron: Gray cast iron delivers excellent vibration damping due to the graphite flake network, which absorbs and disperses mechanical vibrations across the matrix. The compressive strength from 570 MPa to 1,380 MPa makes it one of the most cost-effective materials for heavy compressive load applications. The graphite flake structure acts as a built-in lubricant, improving machinability and reducing tool wear during high-volume production. Ductile Cast Iron: Ductile cast iron provides tensile strength from 400 MPa to 900 MPa, combined with elongation from 2% to 18%, delivering a balance of strength and flexibility absent in other cast iron types. The nodular graphite morphology reduces stress concentrations, increasing fatigue life under cyclic loading. Ductile iron offers a cost advantage over forged steel in many structural applications while maintaining comparable mechanical performance. White Cast Iron: White cast iron provides extreme abrasion resistance due to its continuous iron carbide microstructure, with hardness from 400 HB to 700 HB. The high carbide content significantly extends the service life of wear components in grinding and crushing environments. High-chrome white cast iron grades achieve M₇C₃ carbide hardness from 1,200 HV to 1,600 HV, outperforming standard steels in abrasive wear applications. Malleable Cast Iron: Malleable cast iron provides moderate ductility from 5% to 12% elongation after annealing, allowing it to absorb mechanical stress without sudden fracture. The material is castable into thin sections and complex geometries that are difficult to achieve with ductile iron. Malleable iron's thread-cutting machinability makes it highly suitable for pipe fittings and precision mechanical hardware produced at an industrial scale. Compacted Graphite Iron (CGI): CGI delivers 75% greater tensile strength than gray cast iron while maintaining thermal conductivity from 38 W/m·K to 45 W/m·K, superior to ductile iron. The vermicular graphite structure provides higher fatigue strength from 200 MPa to 280 MPa, supporting high-cycle loading in diesel engine applications. CGI allows component weight reduction compared to gray iron equivalents while meeting higher mechanical performance targets. Alloy Cast Iron: Alloy cast iron extends service life in corrosive, high-temperature, and abrasive environments beyond the capability of standard cast irons. Nickel-alloyed grades resist oxidation up to 1,050°C, while high-silicon grades withstand concentrated acids in chemical processing environments. Chromium-alloyed variants achieve Brinell hardness up to 800 HB, providing wear resistance in pump, liner, and grinding applications where standard materials fail prematurely. events.before: Resources / Materials / Common Types of Synthetic Rubber Common Types of Synthetic Rubber Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 17 min read Published November 25, 2026 Synthetic rubber is a polymer-based elastomer produced through the chemical polymerization of petroleum-derived monomers. Synthetic rubber functions as a group of engineered elastomers formulated to meet specific mechanical, thermal, and chemical performance demands across industrial sectors. The formulations range from general-purpose compounds to specialized grades engineered for extreme temperature, fuel resistance, and weathering conditions. Industries (automotive, aerospace, construction, and medical manufacturing) rely on distinct synthetic rubber types, depending on application load and environmental exposure. The common types of synthetic rubber are listed below. Styrene Butadiene Rubber (SBR) : A copolymer of styrene (23% to 25%) and butadiene, delivering abrasion resistance and tensile strength ranging from 15 to 20 MPa in reinforced form. SBR acts as the standard material in passenger tire treads, conveyor belts, and shoe soles. Nitrile Rubber (NBR) : An acrylonitrile-butadiene copolymer with acrylonitrile content ranging from 18% to 50%, maintaining a service temperature from -40°C to 120°C. NBR acts as the primary elastomer in fuel hoses, O-rings, and oil-resistant gaskets. Neoprene (Polychloroprene) : A polychloroprene-based elastomer offering balanced resistance to weathering, ozone, and moderate chemical exposure. Neoprene retains flexibility across a service temperature range from -40°C to 120°C, finding application in wetsuits, cable jacketing, and industrial hose covers. Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) : A terpolymer of ethylene, propylene, and a diene monomer, operating reliably from -50°C to 150°C. EPDM acts as the dominant elastomer in roofing membranes, automotive door seals, and outdoor weatherstripping. Butyl Rubber (IIR) : An isobutylene-isoprene copolymer with exceptionally low gas permeability, operating from -50°C to 120°C. IIR serves in tubeless tire inner liners, pharmaceutical stoppers, and steam hose applications. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) : A polysiloxane-based elastomer maintaining flexibility across a temperature range from -60°C to 230°C. VMQ serves in medical-grade tubing, aerospace seals, and electronic encapsulation components. Polybutadiene Rubber (BR) : A homopolymer of butadiene with the highest resilience and lowest heat buildup of all synthetic rubber grades, operating from -100°C to 100°C. BR functions as a primary blending component in tire sidewalls and high-impact-resistant polymer systems. 1. Styrene Butadiene Rubber (SBR) Styrene Butadiene Rubber (SBR) is a synthetic rubber copolymer derived from styrene and butadiene monomers, carrying a monomer composition of 23% to 25% styrene and 75% to 77% butadiene. First developed in Germany in 1929 as a substitute for natural rubber, SBR ranks as the most consumed synthetic rubber in global industrial production. The rubber delivers a service temperature range from -40°C to 82°C, with tensile strength reaching 15 to 20 MPa in carbon black-reinforced form. A higher styrene content increases hardness and wear resistance, while a higher butadiene content improves flexibility and low-temperature performance. Primary applications cover passenger tire treads, conveyor belts, shoe soles, flooring, and industrial gaskets, establishing Styrene Butadiene Rubber as a foundational material across automotive and manufacturing sectors. 2. Nitrile Rubber (NBR) Nitrile Rubber (NBR) is a synthetic elastomer produced through the copolymerization of acrylonitrile (ACN) and butadiene, with acrylonitrile content ranging from 15% to 50% depending on the target application. First patented in 1934 by German chemists Erich Konrad and Eduard Tschunkur under the trade name Buna-N, NBR gained widespread industrial adoption due to its resistance to petroleum-based oils, fuels, and chemicals. The acrylonitrile content directly determines oil resistance and gas permeability, where higher ACN concentrations improve chemical resistance but reduce low-temperature flexibility. NBR maintains a service temperature range from -40°C to 120°C, with tensile strength and abrasion resistance suited for high-wear sealing environments. Primary applications cover fuel hoses, O-rings, oil seals, hydraulic gaskets, drilling equipment, and disposable gloves across automotive, oil and gas, aerospace, and medical manufacturing sectors, establishing Nitrile Rubber (NBR) as the dominant oil-resistant elastomer in global industrial production. 3. Neoprene (Polychloroprene) Neoprene is a synthetic elastomer produced through the polymerization of chloroprene (2-chloro-1,3-butadiene), resulting in a polychloroprene polymer with balanced mechanical and chemical performance. First developed in 1930 by American chemist Arnold Collins at DuPont and commercially marketed as Neoprene, the material reached an annual global production of 300,000 tons. The chlorine content in its molecular structure provides inherent flame resistance, moderate oil resistance, and strong ozone and UV stability. Neoprene maintains a service temperature range from -40°C to 121°C, retaining flexibility and structural integrity across outdoor and industrial environments. Primary applications cover wetsuits, cable jacketing, automotive gaskets, industrial conveyor belts, adhesives, and nuclear plant membrane valves, establishing Neoprene as a reliable general-purpose elastomer across marine, construction, and automotive sectors. 4. Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) is a synthetic thermoset rubber composed of ethylene (45% to 85%), propylene, and a non-conjugated diene monomer at 3% to 9%, produced through solution or emulsion polymerization. The saturated hydrocarbon backbone of EPDM delivers outstanding resistance to UV radiation, ozone, weathering, water, and steam, outperforming general-purpose elastomers in outdoor environments. EPDM operates reliably from -50°C to 150°C, maintaining flexibility and sealing integrity across extreme thermal cycles. The diene component provides crosslinking sites for sulfur vulcanization, improving mechanical strength and compression set resistance. Primary applications cover roofing membranes, automotive door and window seals, wire and cable insulation, and industrial hose systems, positioning Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) as the dominant elastomer in weathering-critical engineering applications. 5. Butyl Rubber (IIR) Butyl Rubber (IIR) is a synthetic elastomer produced through low-temperature cationic copolymerization of isobutylene ( 98%) with a small amount of isoprene ( 2%), forming an isobutylene-isoprene rubber with a predominantly saturated backbone. IIR holds the distinction of being the known elastomer that does not transmit gases, delivering exceptionally low gas and moisture permeability across industrial sealing applications developed in 1937. The saturated backbone structure provides outstanding resistance to ozone, UV radiation, heat aging, and dilute acids and alkalis, with a service temperature range from -50°C to 120°C. Halogenated grades (CIIR and BIIR) developed in the 1960s further improved curing rates and adhesion properties. Primary applications cover tubeless tire inner liners, pharmaceutical vial stoppers, steam hoses, gas-tight membranes, and construction sealants, establishing Butyl Rubber (IIR) as the standard elastomer in airtight and moisture-barrier engineering systems. 6. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) Silicone Rubber (VMQ), formally designated as Vinyl Methyl Silicone, is a polysiloxane-based elastomer composed of silicon, oxygen, carbon, and hydrogen, forming a high molecular weight polymer backbone with vinyl groups added to improve crosslinking and mechanical performance. VMQ carries an inorganic siloxane backbone that delivers thermal stability across a service temperature range from -60°C to 230°C, with specialty grades extending performance beyond 300°C, unlike carbon-based elastomers. VMQ maintains flexibility, electrical insulation, and chemical resistance across cryogenic and high-temperature environments where organic rubbers fail. Its biocompatibility, odorless nature, and non-toxicity qualify it for food-grade, pharmaceutical, and medical-grade applications. Primary applications cover aerospace seals, medical tubing, electronic encapsulation, automotive engine gaskets, and food processing components, establishing Silicone Rubber (VMQ) as the preferred high-performance elastomer in temperature-critical and biocompatible engineering systems. 7. Polybutadiene Rubber (BR) Polybutadiene Rubber (BR) is a synthetic elastomer produced through solution polymerization of 1,3-butadiene, yielding a high cis-1,4-microstructure content of 90% to 98% that governs its elastic and mechanical performance. BR ranks as the second most consumed synthetic rubber globally, with annual demand exceeding 2.8 million metric tons, driven by the tire industry, which accounts for over 70% of total BR consumption. The glass transition temperature ranges from -95°C to -110°C, giving BR the highest low-temperature flexibility among commercial synthetic rubbers. Its low heat buildup, superior resilience, and crack growth resistance make it the dominant blending component in tire tread and sidewall compounds. Primary applications cover passenger tire compounds, golf ball cores, conveyor belts, shoe soles, and high-impact ABS plastic modification, establishing Polybutadiene Rubber (BR) as a foundational elastomer in high-resilience and wear-critical industrial systems. How Do the Different Types of Synthetic Rubber Compare in Performance? The performance of synthetic rubber types varies significantly across temperature tolerance, chemical resistance, weathering durability, and cost. Each elastomer grade carries a distinct property profile that determines its suitability across automotive, industrial, medical, and construction applications. Selecting the correct synthetic rubber grade depends on the operating environment, chemical exposure, and mechanical load requirements. Silicone (VMQ) leads the widest temperature range from -60°C to 230°C, while Nitrile Butadiene Rubber (NBR) holds the strongest oil resistance rating among all grades. Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) and Butyl (IIR) deliver the highest weathering resistance, favoring outdoor and airtight sealing applications. SBR and BR carry the lowest cost index, dominating high-volume tire and footwear manufacturing sectors. The different types of synthetic rubber compared in performance are shown in the table below. Which Type of Synthetic Rubber Has the Best Heat Resistance? The types of synthetic rubber that have the best heat resistance are listed below. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) : The highest heat-resistant synthetic rubber grade, maintaining flexibility from -60°C to 230°C, with specialty formulations exceeding 300°C in aerospace and medical sealing applications. Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) : Operates from -50°C to 150°C, retaining ozone and weathering resistance at elevated temperatures across outdoor and automotive sealing systems. Neoprene (Polychloroprene) : Sustains a service temperature from -40°C to 121°C with retained flame and ozone resistance, suiting cable jacketing and industrial belting applications. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber (NBR) : Operates from -40°C to 120°C, combining oil resistance with adequate thermal stability in fuel and hydraulic sealing environments. Butyl Rubber (IIR) : Maintains performance from -50°C to 120°C with strong resistance to thermal oxidation in steam hose and pharmaceutical closure applications. Styrene Butadiene Rubber (SBR) : Operates from -40°C to 82°C, limited in high-temperature applications but dominant in tire treads and conveyor belt systems. Polybutadiene Rubber (BR) : The lowest upper heat threshold at 100°C, compensating with the highest low-temperature flexibility at -95°C in tire sidewall and polymer blending applications. Which Synthetic Rubber is Most Resistant to Chemicals? The most resistant synthetic rubbers to chemicals are listed below. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber (NBR) : The strongest oil and fuel-resistant grade, withstanding petroleum-based oils, gasoline, diesel, and hydraulic fluids across acrylonitrile content ranging from 18% to 50%. Neoprene (Polychloroprene) : Delivers moderate resistance to oils, greases, acids, and refrigerants, with chlorine content providing inherent chemical stability across a broad exposure range. Butyl Rubber (IIR) : Resistant to acids, alkalis, polar solvents, and ketone-based hydraulic fluids, performing poorly against petroleum-based oils and hydrocarbon solvents. Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) : Resistant to water, steam, polar solvents, and dilute acids, performing poorly against petroleum-based oils and hydrocarbon fuels. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) : Resistant to dilute acids, alkalis, ozone, and UV exposure, with limited resistance to concentrated acids, fuels, and hydrocarbon solvents. Styrene Butadiene Rubber (SBR) : Resistant to water, dilute acids, and alcohols, showing poor resistance to oils, fuels, and concentrated chemical agents. Polybutadiene Rubber (BR) : The lowest chemical resistance among major grades, offering adequate performance against water and dilute inorganic acids. What Are the Main Uses of Synthetic Rubber Across Industries? The main uses of synthetic rubber across industries are listed below. Automotive Industry : Synthetic rubber serves in fuel hoses, oil seals, door seals, timing belts, and tire compounds across passenger and commercial vehicle production. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber dominates oil-contact components, while Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer covers weatherstripping and door seals. Tire Manufacturing : Styrene Butadiene Rubber and Polybutadiene Rubber function as the primary compounds in tire treads and sidewalls, accounting for over 70% of global Polybutadiene Rubber consumption. Butyl Rubber (IIR) serves exclusively in tubeless tire inner liners due to its unmatched gas impermeability. Aerospace and Defense : Silicone Rubber (VMQ) and specialty fluorosilicone grades seal fuel tanks, hydraulic systems, and structural joints operating across extreme temperature ranges. Neoprene serves in self-sealing fuel tank liners and cable jacketing across military and aviation platforms. Construction and Infrastructure : Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer dominates roofing membrane systems, expansion joint seals, and waterproofing layers in commercial building structures. Butyl Rubber serves in construction sealants, flashing tapes, and gas-tight membrane systems requiring long-term weather resistance. Medical and Pharmaceutical : Silicone Rubber (VMQ) provides biocompatible tubing, seals, and encapsulation components across medical device and surgical equipment production. Butyl Rubber (IIR) functions as the standard pharmaceutical vial stopper material due to its chemical inertness and gas impermeability. Oil and Gas Industry : Nitrile Butadiene Rubber serves in blowout preventers, packers, drilling equipment seals, and pipeline gaskets exposed to hydrocarbons and elevated pressure. Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer covers above-ground sealing systems exposed to weathering and steam in refinery environments. Electronics and Electrical Systems : Silicone Rubber (VMQ) provides wire and cable insulation, connector seals, and electromagnetic interference shielding across industrial and consumer electronics manufacturing. Styrene Butadiene Rubber serves in cable insulation and electrical gasket applications requiring moderate chemical resistance at a lower cost. How Is Synthetic Rubber Used in the Automotive Industry? Synthetic rubber serves in the automotive industry as a primary material for sealing, vibration damping, fuel management, and structural bonding components. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber covers fuel hoses, oil seals, and O-rings due to its resistance to petroleum-based fluids, while Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer covers door seals, window weatherstripping, and radiator hoses from -50°C to 150°C. Neoprene provides transmission belts, engine mounts, and vibration isolators where moderate oil and heat resistance are required simultaneously. Styrene Butadiene Rubber and Polybutadiene Rubber form the primary tire tread and sidewall compounds, with Polybutadiene Rubber accounting for over 70% of tire sidewall elastomer consumption globally. Butyl Rubber (IIR) serves in tubeless tire inner liners, retaining air pressure and minimizing steel belt corrosion due to its gas impermeability. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) covers high-temperature engine gaskets, ignition cable insulation, and sensor seals operating continuously above 150°C in modern internal combustion and electric vehicle systems. How Is Synthetic Rubber Used in Medical and Healthcare Applications? Synthetic rubber is used in medical and healthcare applications as a primary material for biocompatible sealing, fluid management, protective equipment, and implantable device components. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) dominates medical-grade applications due to its biocompatibility, non-toxicity, and thermal stability from -60°C to 230°C, meeting FDA, USP Class VI, and ISO 10993 certification standards. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber serves in disposable examination gloves, surgical gloves, and laboratory protective gear, replacing natural latex due to its lower allergenic risk and puncture resistance across acrylonitrile content ranging from 18% to 50%. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) provides medical-grade tubing, catheters, implant-grade sheeting, and drainage systems where long-term biological compatibility and sterilization resistance are required. Butyl Rubber (IIR) functions as the standard pharmaceutical vial and injection stopper material, maintaining gas impermeability and chemical inertness across repeated needle penetration cycles. Silicone-based implants cover reconstructive and corrective medical procedures requiring durable, flexible, and non-reactive materials in direct tissue contact environments. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber further extends into laboratory tubing, fluid transfer lines, and diagnostic equipment seals across clinical and research healthcare facilities. Is Synthetic Rubber Safe for Food Contact Applications? Yes, synthetic rubber is safe for food contact applications. The safety rating depends on the grade, formulation, and regulatory certification of the elastomer. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) functions as the primary food-contact elastomer, meeting FDA 21 CFR, EU 10/2011, and NSF 51 certification standards across baking mats, food processing seals, and beverage tubing. Butyl Rubber (IIR) qualifies for food-contact closures in pharmaceutical and food-grade bottle stopper applications due to its chemical inertness and odorless composition. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber requires specific food-grade compounding certification before qualifying for direct food contact, as residual acrylonitrile content above permissible limits disqualifies standard industrial grades. Styrene Butadiene Rubber, Neoprene, and Polybutadiene Rubber carry limited food-contact suitability, requiring independent formulation testing and regulatory approval, depending on additive composition and intended application. How to Choose the Right Type of Synthetic Rubber for a Specific Application? To choose the right type of synthetic rubber for a specific application, follow the seven steps listed below. Identify the Operating Temperature Range . Determine the minimum and maximum service temperatures the elastomer encounters. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) suits extreme ranges from -60°C to 230°C, while Styrene Butadiene Rubber covers moderate ranges from -40°C to 82°C. Evaluate Chemical Exposure Requirements . Identify the specific chemicals, fluids, and solvents the elastomer contacts during service. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber suits petroleum-based oil and fuel exposure, while Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer suits water, steam, and polar solvent environments. Assess Mechanical Load and Wear Conditions . Determine the pressure, friction, and dynamic stress levels the elastomer must withstand continuously. Polybutadiene Rubber suits high-resilience applications, while Butyl Rubber (IIR) suits low-dynamic, high-damping sealing systems. Determine Weathering and UV Exposure Levels . Evaluate whether the elastomer faces prolonged outdoor exposure to ozone, UV radiation, and moisture. Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer and Butyl Rubber (IIR) deliver the highest weathering resistance among major synthetic rubber grades. Check Regulatory and Safety Certification Requirements . Confirm whether the application requires food-grade, medical-grade, or industry-specific compliance certifications. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) meets FDA 21 CFR, USP Class VI, and NSF 51 standards for food contact and medical device applications. Compare Cost Index Against Performance Requirements . Balance material cost against the mechanical and chemical performance demands of the application. Styrene Butadiene Rubber and Polybutadiene Rubber carry the lowest cost index, while Silicone Rubber (VMQ) carries the highest. Validate Through Application-Specific Testing . Conduct compression set, tensile strength, chemical swell, and aging resistance testing before full-scale deployment. Validation testing confirms elastomer suitability across the actual service conditions of the application. What Factors Affect the Performance of Synthetic Rubber in Extreme Conditions? The factors that affect the performance of synthetic rubber in extreme conditions are temperature extremes, chemical concentration, UV exposure duration, and mechanical compression. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) retains flexibility from -60°C to 230°C, while Styrene Butadiene Rubber loses mechanical integrity above 82°C under continuous thermal load. Styrene Butadiene Rubber and Nitrile Butadiene Rubber show measurable surface cracking after 500 to 1,000 hours of outdoor UV exposure without protective additives. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber at 50% acrylonitrile content retains dimensional stability in full-concentration petroleum fluid immersion, while lower acrylonitrile grades swell beyond acceptable limits above 40% fluid concentration. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) maintains the lowest long-term compression set among major synthetic rubber grades, retaining sealing integrity across repeated thermal cycling in aerospace and medical device applications. What Is the Cost Range for Different Types of Synthetic Rubber? The cost range for different types of synthetic rubber spans from [$ 1.50 to $ 45.00] per kilogram, varying from commodity-grade elastomers to specialty high-performance compounds. Styrene Butadiene Rubber and Polybutadiene Rubber carry the lowest market price, ranging from [$ 1.50 to $ 2.50] per kilogram, reflecting their petroleum-derived monomer availability and high-volume production scale. events.after: Resources / Materials / Common Types of Synthetic Rubber Common Types of Synthetic Rubber Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 17 min read Published November 25, 2026 Synthetic rubber is a polymer-based elastomer produced through the chemical polymerization of petroleum-derived monomers. Synthetic rubber functions as a group of engineered elastomers formulated to meet specific mechanical, thermal, and chemical performance demands across industrial sectors. The formulations range from general-purpose compounds to specialized grades engineered for extreme temperature, fuel resistance, and weathering conditions. Industries (automotive, aerospace, construction, and medical manufacturing) rely on distinct synthetic rubber types, depending on application load and environmental exposure. The common types of synthetic rubber are listed below. Styrene Butadiene Rubber (SBR) : A copolymer of styrene (23% to 25%) and butadiene, delivering abrasion resistance and tensile strength ranging from 15 to 20 MPa in reinforced form. SBR acts as the standard material in passenger tire treads, conveyor belts, and shoe soles. Nitrile Rubber (NBR) : An acrylonitrile-butadiene copolymer with acrylonitrile content ranging from 18% to 50%, maintaining a service temperature from -40°C to 120°C. NBR acts as the primary elastomer in fuel hoses, O-rings, and oil-resistant gaskets. Neoprene (Polychloroprene) : A polychloroprene-based elastomer offering balanced resistance to weathering, ozone, and moderate chemical exposure. Neoprene retains flexibility across a service temperature range from -40°C to 120°C, finding application in wetsuits, cable jacketing, and industrial hose covers. Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) : A terpolymer of ethylene, propylene, and a diene monomer, operating reliably from -50°C to 150°C. EPDM acts as the dominant elastomer in roofing membranes, automotive door seals, and outdoor weatherstripping. Butyl Rubber (IIR) : An isobutylene-isoprene copolymer with exceptionally low gas permeability, operating from -50°C to 120°C. IIR serves in tubeless tire inner liners, pharmaceutical stoppers, and steam hose applications. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) : A polysiloxane-based elastomer maintaining flexibility across a temperature range from -60°C to 230°C. VMQ serves in medical-grade tubing, aerospace seals, and electronic encapsulation components. Polybutadiene Rubber (BR) : A homopolymer of butadiene with the highest resilience and lowest heat buildup of all synthetic rubber grades, operating from -100°C to 100°C. BR functions as a primary blending component in tire sidewalls and high-impact-resistant polymer systems. 1. Styrene Butadiene Rubber (SBR) Styrene Butadiene Rubber (SBR) is a synthetic rubber copolymer derived from styrene and butadiene monomers, carrying a monomer composition of 23% to 25% styrene and 75% to 77% butadiene. First developed in Germany in 1929 as a substitute for natural rubber, SBR ranks as the most consumed synthetic rubber in global industrial production. The rubber delivers a service temperature range from -40°C to 82°C, with tensile strength reaching 15 to 20 MPa in carbon black-reinforced form. A higher styrene content increases hardness and wear resistance, while a higher butadiene content improves flexibility and low-temperature performance. Primary applications cover passenger tire treads, conveyor belts, shoe soles, flooring, and industrial gaskets, establishing Styrene Butadiene Rubber as a foundational material across automotive and manufacturing sectors. 2. Nitrile Rubber (NBR) Nitrile Rubber (NBR) is a synthetic elastomer produced through the copolymerization of acrylonitrile (ACN) and butadiene, with acrylonitrile content ranging from 15% to 50% depending on the target application. First patented in 1934 by German chemists Erich Konrad and Eduard Tschunkur under the trade name Buna-N, NBR gained widespread industrial adoption due to its resistance to petroleum-based oils, fuels, and chemicals. The acrylonitrile content directly determines oil resistance and gas permeability, where higher ACN concentrations improve chemical resistance but reduce low-temperature flexibility. NBR maintains a service temperature range from -40°C to 120°C, with tensile strength and abrasion resistance suited for high-wear sealing environments. Primary applications cover fuel hoses, O-rings, oil seals, hydraulic gaskets, drilling equipment, and disposable gloves across automotive, oil and gas, aerospace, and medical manufacturing sectors, establishing Nitrile Rubber (NBR) as the dominant oil-resistant elastomer in global industrial production. 3. Neoprene (Polychloroprene) Neoprene is a synthetic elastomer produced through the polymerization of chloroprene (2-chloro-1,3-butadiene), resulting in a polychloroprene polymer with balanced mechanical and chemical performance. First developed in 1930 by American chemist Arnold Collins at DuPont and commercially marketed as Neoprene, the material reached an annual global production of 300,000 tons. The chlorine content in its molecular structure provides inherent flame resistance, moderate oil resistance, and strong ozone and UV stability. Neoprene maintains a service temperature range from -40°C to 121°C, retaining flexibility and structural integrity across outdoor and industrial environments. Primary applications cover wetsuits, cable jacketing, automotive gaskets, industrial conveyor belts, adhesives, and nuclear plant membrane valves, establishing Neoprene as a reliable general-purpose elastomer across marine, construction, and automotive sectors. 4. Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) is a synthetic thermoset rubber composed of ethylene (45% to 85%), propylene, and a non-conjugated diene monomer at 3% to 9%, produced through solution or emulsion polymerization. The saturated hydrocarbon backbone of EPDM delivers outstanding resistance to UV radiation, ozone, weathering, water, and steam, outperforming general-purpose elastomers in outdoor environments. EPDM operates reliably from -50°C to 150°C, maintaining flexibility and sealing integrity across extreme thermal cycles. The diene component provides crosslinking sites for sulfur vulcanization, improving mechanical strength and compression set resistance. Primary applications cover roofing membranes, automotive door and window seals, wire and cable insulation, and industrial hose systems, positioning Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) as the dominant elastomer in weathering-critical engineering applications. 5. Butyl Rubber (IIR) Butyl Rubber (IIR) is a synthetic elastomer produced through low-temperature cationic copolymerization of isobutylene ( 98%) with a small amount of isoprene ( 2%), forming an isobutylene-isoprene rubber with a predominantly saturated backbone. IIR holds the distinction of being the known elastomer that does not transmit gases, delivering exceptionally low gas and moisture permeability across industrial sealing applications developed in 1937. The saturated backbone structure provides outstanding resistance to ozone, UV radiation, heat aging, and dilute acids and alkalis, with a service temperature range from -50°C to 120°C. Halogenated grades (CIIR and BIIR) developed in the 1960s further improved curing rates and adhesion properties. Primary applications cover tubeless tire inner liners, pharmaceutical vial stoppers, steam hoses, gas-tight membranes, and construction sealants, establishing Butyl Rubber (IIR) as the standard elastomer in airtight and moisture-barrier engineering systems. 6. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) Silicone Rubber (VMQ), formally designated as Vinyl Methyl Silicone, is a polysiloxane-based elastomer composed of silicon, oxygen, carbon, and hydrogen, forming a high molecular weight polymer backbone with vinyl groups added to improve crosslinking and mechanical performance. VMQ carries an inorganic siloxane backbone that delivers thermal stability across a service temperature range from -60°C to 230°C, with specialty grades extending performance beyond 300°C, unlike carbon-based elastomers. VMQ maintains flexibility, electrical insulation, and chemical resistance across cryogenic and high-temperature environments where organic rubbers fail. Its biocompatibility, odorless nature, and non-toxicity qualify it for food-grade, pharmaceutical, and medical-grade applications. Primary applications cover aerospace seals, medical tubing, electronic encapsulation, automotive engine gaskets, and food processing components, establishing Silicone Rubber (VMQ) as the preferred high-performance elastomer in temperature-critical and biocompatible engineering systems. 7. Polybutadiene Rubber (BR) Polybutadiene Rubber (BR) is a synthetic elastomer produced through solution polymerization of 1,3-butadiene, yielding a high cis-1,4-microstructure content of 90% to 98% that governs its elastic and mechanical performance. BR ranks as the second most consumed synthetic rubber globally, with annual demand exceeding 2.8 million metric tons, driven by the tire industry, which accounts for over 70% of total BR consumption. The glass transition temperature ranges from -95°C to -110°C, giving BR the highest low-temperature flexibility among commercial synthetic rubbers. Its low heat buildup, superior resilience, and crack growth resistance make it the dominant blending component in tire tread and sidewall compounds. Primary applications cover passenger tire compounds, golf ball cores, conveyor belts, shoe soles, and high-impact ABS plastic modification, establishing Polybutadiene Rubber (BR) as a foundational elastomer in high-resilience and wear-critical industrial systems. How Do the Different Types of Synthetic Rubber Compare in Performance? The performance of synthetic rubber types varies significantly across temperature tolerance, chemical resistance, weathering durability, and cost. Each elastomer grade carries a distinct property profile that determines its suitability across automotive, industrial, medical, and construction applications. Selecting the correct synthetic rubber grade depends on the operating environment, chemical exposure, and mechanical load requirements. Silicone (VMQ) leads the widest temperature range from -60°C to 230°C, while Nitrile Butadiene Rubber (NBR) holds the strongest oil resistance rating among all grades. Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) and Butyl (IIR) deliver the highest weathering resistance, favoring outdoor and airtight sealing applications. SBR and BR carry the lowest cost index, dominating high-volume tire and footwear manufacturing sectors. The different types of synthetic rubber compared in performance are shown in the table below. Which Type of Synthetic Rubber Has the Best Heat Resistance? The types of synthetic rubber that have the best heat resistance are listed below. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) : The highest heat-resistant synthetic rubber grade, maintaining flexibility from -60°C to 230°C, with specialty formulations exceeding 300°C in aerospace and medical sealing applications. Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) : Operates from -50°C to 150°C, retaining ozone and weathering resistance at elevated temperatures across outdoor and automotive sealing systems. Neoprene (Polychloroprene) : Sustains a service temperature from -40°C to 121°C with retained flame and ozone resistance, suiting cable jacketing and industrial belting applications. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber (NBR) : Operates from -40°C to 120°C, combining oil resistance with adequate thermal stability in fuel and hydraulic sealing environments. Butyl Rubber (IIR) : Maintains performance from -50°C to 120°C with strong resistance to thermal oxidation in steam hose and pharmaceutical closure applications. Styrene Butadiene Rubber (SBR) : Operates from -40°C to 82°C, limited in high-temperature applications but dominant in tire treads and conveyor belt systems. Polybutadiene Rubber (BR) : The lowest upper heat threshold at 100°C, compensating with the highest low-temperature flexibility at -95°C in tire sidewall and polymer blending applications. Which Synthetic Rubber is Most Resistant to Chemicals? The most resistant synthetic rubbers to chemicals are listed below. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber (NBR) : The strongest oil and fuel-resistant grade, withstanding petroleum-based oils, gasoline, diesel, and hydraulic fluids across acrylonitrile content ranging from 18% to 50%. Neoprene (Polychloroprene) : Delivers moderate resistance to oils, greases, acids, and refrigerants, with chlorine content providing inherent chemical stability across a broad exposure range. Butyl Rubber (IIR) : Resistant to acids, alkalis, polar solvents, and ketone-based hydraulic fluids, performing poorly against petroleum-based oils and hydrocarbon solvents. Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) : Resistant to water, steam, polar solvents, and dilute acids, performing poorly against petroleum-based oils and hydrocarbon fuels. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) : Resistant to dilute acids, alkalis, ozone, and UV exposure, with limited resistance to concentrated acids, fuels, and hydrocarbon solvents. Styrene Butadiene Rubber (SBR) : Resistant to water, dilute acids, and alcohols, showing poor resistance to oils, fuels, and concentrated chemical agents. Polybutadiene Rubber (BR) : The lowest chemical resistance among major grades, offering adequate performance against water and dilute inorganic acids. Butyl Rubber (IIR) serves exclusively in tubeless tire inner liners due to its unmatched gas impermeability. Neoprene serves in self-sealing fuel tank liners and cable jacketing across military and aviation platforms. Butyl Rubber (IIR) functions as the standard pharmaceutical vial stopper material due to its chemical inertness and gas impermeability. Oil and Gas Industry : Nitrile Butadiene Rubber serves in blowout preventers, packers, drilling equipment seals, and pipeline gaskets exposed to hydrocarbons and elevated pressure. Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer covers above-ground sealing systems exposed to weathering and steam in refinery environments. Electronics and Electrical Systems : Silicone Rubber (VMQ) provides wire and cable insulation, connector seals, and electromagnetic interference shielding across industrial and consumer electronics manufacturing. Styrene Butadiene Rubber serves in cable insulation and electrical gasket applications requiring moderate chemical resistance at a lower cost. How Is Synthetic Rubber Used in the Automotive Industry? Synthetic rubber serves in the automotive industry as a primary material for sealing, vibration damping, fuel management, and structural bonding components. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber covers fuel hoses, oil seals, and O-rings due to its resistance to petroleum-based fluids, while Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer covers door seals, window weatherstripping, and radiator hoses from -50°C to 150°C. Neoprene provides transmission belts, engine mounts, and vibration isolators where moderate oil and heat resistance are required simultaneously. Styrene Butadiene Rubber and Polybutadiene Rubber form the primary tire tread and sidewall compounds, with Polybutadiene Rubber accounting for over 70% of tire sidewall elastomer consumption globally. Butyl Rubber (IIR) serves in tubeless tire inner liners, retaining air pressure and minimizing steel belt corrosion due to its gas impermeability. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) covers high-temperature engine gaskets, ignition cable insulation, and sensor seals operating continuously above 150°C in modern internal combustion and electric vehicle systems. How Is Synthetic Rubber Used in Medical and Healthcare Applications? Synthetic rubber is used in medical and healthcare applications as a primary material for biocompatible sealing, fluid management, protective equipment, and implantable device components. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) dominates medical-grade applications due to its biocompatibility, non-toxicity, and thermal stability from -60°C to 230°C, meeting FDA, USP Class VI, and ISO 10993 certification standards. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber serves in disposable examination gloves, surgical gloves, and laboratory protective gear, replacing natural latex due to its lower allergenic risk and puncture resistance across acrylonitrile content ranging from 18% to 50%. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) provides medical-grade tubing, catheters, implant-grade sheeting, and drainage systems where long-term biological compatibility and sterilization resistance are required. Butyl Rubber (IIR) functions as the standard pharmaceutical vial and injection stopper material, maintaining gas impermeability and chemical inertness across repeated needle penetration cycles. Styrene Butadiene Rubber, Neoprene, and Polybutadiene Rubber carry limited food-contact suitability, requiring independent formulation testing and regulatory approval, depending on additive composition and intended application.
